items.body: Review by AshleyLarksTongue — This album is quite an acquired taste. I hated it at first, and hated it even more every listen after. It took me 20 listens before I started even tolerating it. However, after 30 listens, I can say it's a masterpiece of avant-prog. The Captain's voice has really grown on me, and so has the wonderful musicianship. My favorite track and the most essential track off of this album is sweet sweet bulbs. I really have no idea how to say more about this album because it is simply indescribable. I'm looking forward to exploring some more of Beefheart's works. And everyone around me now has to deal with me doing my impression of the hilarious vocals on this album.
items._genre: avant-garde / experimental rock / outsider music
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以极度反叛的姿态解构了传统摇滚的结构框架，将自由爵士、布鲁斯与先锋噪音熔于一炉，形成碎片化、棱角分明的声响图景。Captain Beefheart 的演唱方式充满原始表现力，带有戏剧化的嘶吼与即兴口语化表达，配以魔幻的双吉他对话和多层次复合节奏，构成了极为密集的听觉挑战。乐评人经历了从排斥到接纳的漫长过程，约三十次聆听后逐渐感受到其内在的严密逻辑与高超的器乐演奏水准。这种先拒后纳的接受曲线本身也说明作品具有远超表面噪音的纵深，等待耐心发掘后展现出前卫摇滚史上罕见的整体构思与即兴天赋。

items.body: Some promotion arrives generously late, but with this debut album by the Australian solo project Empty Vessel, I felt it was more than necessary to give it some attention anyway. Tom Wojcicki is an artist unknown to most, who released the album “Ruin Value” in the spring of 2025, an opus consisting of eight tracks. What I hear here defies all imagination: an absolute masterpiece in which the artist blends Industrial, Cinematic, and Ritual elements in a remarkably refined manner. He creates a tormented atmosphere of overwhelming sounds, with percussion effects that reverberate like drones. That overwhelming quality, in particular, is almost indescribable. Rarely have I encountered an artist capable of creating sounds as intense, present, and tormented as those of Empty Vessel. The tracks can be repetitive at times, but because of their sheer intensity, you are truly blown away. Before you know it, you are trapped in a sonic web of terrifying and illusory images. The album is a succession of insane tracks, meaning that you discover one highlight after another. If you are a fan of the genres mentioned above and are not yet familiar with Empty Vessel, I would simply recommend buying this album without listening to it beforehand. An absolute masterpiece, and it will not be easy to follow this up with an equally powerful successor. (Rating:9). Listen to “Scattered Pieces Of Her”: Scattered Pieces Of Her by Empty Vessel About Empty Vessel Empty Vessel is the solo industrial and power electronics project of Australian artist Tom Wojcicki. “Ruin Value” was released on 14 April 2025 through the German label Dunkelheit Produktionen as a hand-numbered CD limited to 200 copies with a 4-page booklet, plus a digital edition, under catalog number DP179CD. The album runs eight tracks, opening with “Scattered Pieces Of Her” and closing with “Zero Fetish”. Empty Vessel has also recorded under the names Droid Sector, Broken Fingers, Glass Barbeque, Aurora Seven and Cockroach Diocese. “Ruin Value” is Empty Vessel’s first release to be reviewed on Side-Line.
items._genre: industrial / power electronics / dark ambient / cinematic
items._cn_summary: 澳大利亚单人项目Empty Vessel首张专辑将工业、电影化与仪式元素熔于一炉，八首作品构建出极具压迫感的声响图景。Tom Wojcicki以鼓击效果模拟持续嗡鸣的无人机频率，在反复循环的节奏中不断叠加张力，使听者陷入由恐怖意象与幻觉画面交织而成的声场。专辑呈现出一连串高密度曲目，从开篇的《Scattered Pieces Of Her》到终曲的《Zero Fetish》，每一首都维持着高度的强度与不安感。该作由德国地下厂牌Dunkelheit Produktionen于2025年4月发行，限量200张编号CD附四页手册，凸显其手工制作与地下流通属性。项目此前曾以Droid Sector、Broken Fingers等多个名号录制作品，体现出艺术家在极端电子领域的持续探索。

items.body: (Photo credit: Allen Cohen) Reaching Marlboro requires a gradual surrender of scale. Roads narrow, familiar coordinates loosen, and the forest exerts its own editorial influence, stripping away whatever feels extraneous until distance becomes a form of concentration. On September 20, 2026, that concentration gathered inside Ragle Hall at the Serkin Center, where the Marlboro Music Artist Residency Program presented The World of György Kurtág, an arresting sequence of works composed or arranged for soprano and double bass. Beyond the hall stood the wooded seclusion of southern Vermont; within it, soprano Lucy Fitz Gibbon and bassist William Langlie Miletich moved between Sprechstimme, art song, extended technique, and charged silence. Seclusion mattered because Kurtág’s music alters the proportions of attention. The claim embedded in the program’s title was stranger than its apparent simplicity suggested. The phrase “world of” ordinarily announces breadth, an oeuvre surveyed from above. Kurtág offers no such cartographic comfort. His world emerges through radical compression, forming under pressure between a sound and its possible disappearance. A few pitches can contain the moral weight of a dramatic scene. A pause can bend duration until time folds inward, secreting another time inside itself. His miniatures remain small only to the clock. To enter them is to accept unfamiliar laws under which fragments carry the mass of vanished wholes and inhalation behaves as active matter. The surrounding forest supplied an uncannily precise grammar for this experience. Every trunk concealed years in concentric script; every root continued a sentence underground. Kurtág’s art operates within a related economy of the imperceptible. A phrase ends, yet its pressure travels elsewhere. Music becomes the audible extremity of processes occurring beneath language. The sequence approached that hidden economy gently through Lembit Beecher’s With Grandchildren, drawn from his 2014 cycle Looking at Spring: Meditations on Aging. The larger work grew from interviews librettist Liza Balkan conducted with senior citizens in Toronto and central Vermont, making its appearance in Marlboro feel almost homeward. Their voices had passed into text and music before returning to the region transformed, bearing traces of their speakers without claiming to preserve them intact. Harmonics in the bass courted a rocking motion whose comfort never became secure, while Fitz Gibbon searched amid the delicate failures of memory. The soul became an unfinished sentence poised beneath scissors, family albums reduced to particles of touch and chronology. Bone creaked as marrow acquired a secret literacy, becoming a divining instrument for the inaccessible past. Beecher respected recollection as an unstable act in which forgetting shapes experience as decisively as retention. Miletich’s pale overtones gave the bass an elderly nervous system of its own. The final word escaped capture, suspending language where recognition touches disappearance. John Cage’s The Wonderful Widow of Eighteen Springs opened another passage into that borderland. Composed in 1942, its text comes from a nocturnal passage concerning Isobel in Finnegans Wake, a book of sleeping consciousness and linguistic mutation. Cage answered that abundance with severe economy. The voice circles within three pitches, while the original accompaniment is played on a closed piano tapped by the player. In Marlboro, those impulses migrated to the double bass, where Miletich turned his instrument of choice into a hollow nocturnal chamber. What had once been struck wood surrounding dormant strings now came from an assemblage held against the player’s body, each impact becoming a coded knock from somewhere inside itself. Fitz Gibbon sustained Cage’s narrow compass with remarkable intensity. Repetition wandered in place, circling a road inferred from every failed attempt to leave it. James Joyce’s words acquired the phosphorescence of objects glimpsed among trees. Isobel became a consciousness translated into the landscape, as identity passed into leaf matter and the boundary between a sleeping mind and the forest dreaming it lost authority. Amy Beth Kirsten’s yes I said yes I will Yes followed as a second excavation of Joyce, drawing on Molly Bloom’s concluding monologue in Ulysses. Written in 2012 for soprano and contrabass, with the bassist also vocalizing, it entered an illuminating dialogue with Cage. Both composers extract a concentrated vocal world from Joyce’s literary machinery. Whereas Cage cools language toward incantation, Kirsten restores its heat while fracturing the body that generates it. Isobel’s suspension yields to Molly’s consciousness in bed, where memory moves through eros and resistance before reaching the irrevocable “Yes.” Fitz Gibbon and Miletich rendered that sensuality as a condition divided against itself. Pizzicato entered beside Miletich’s droning hum, while glissandi bent the music from stable coordinates. Fitz Gibbon inhabited desire while observing its mechanisms from afar, consciousness hovering above its own flesh. The deeply inflected conclusion unfolded as slow-motion blues, each pitch bearing the drag of pleasure becoming memory before experience could have its say. These works prepared the ear for Kurtág’s Einige Sätze aus den Sudelbüchern Georg Christoph Lichtenbergs, Op. 37a, begun in 1996 and expanded for soprano and double bass in 1999. The cycle arose from his encounter with the private notebooks of Georg Christoph Lichtenberg, the 18th-century physicist whose intellect moved between experiment and satire. Never intended for publication, these “waste books” gathered observations whose brevity sharpened their reach. Lichtenberg’s scrutiny ranges across provincialism and religion, colonialism and literary history. Each joke becomes a trapdoor opening onto centuries of vanity. Kurtág began setting the aphorisms while ill, initially for solo soprano. Singer Maria Husmann encouraged the addition of double bass after experimenting with improvised accompaniment, a genesis audible in the finished cycle. Voice and instrument discover one another without settling into fixed roles. The bass accompanies before interrupting, then places a dark question mark beneath Lichtenberg’s wit. Fitz Gibbon and Miletich inhabited these relations with theatrical aptitude. The opening “Die Kartoffeln” (“The Potatoes”) was oddly beautiful in its evocation of slumbering tubers and their potential afterlife. “Kirchtürme” (“Church Spires”) rose through lovely pizzicato, its aspiration destabilized by the plucking that produced it. “Koan” became a fervent prayer edging toward cognitive seizure. Kurtág exposed the nervous system inside each of these, revealing the involuntary twitch beneath polished intelligence. That method reached sardonic clarity in “…und eine neue Welt…” (“…and a New World…”), where Fitz Gibbon sang through her teeth: “The American who discovered Columbus made a nasty discovery.” The reversal compresses colonial history into a grammatical ambush, exposing discovery as a story power tells about intrusion. Here, as elsewhere in the cycle, language appeared to turn against the assumptions concealed within its own syntax. Beecher’s stop-motion films, still a work in progress and therefore accompanying only selected aphorisms, extended this instability into a visual register. His reappearance as animator also gave the program a satisfying circular architecture. Having entered through his own music in With Grandchildren, he returned within Kurtág’s, translating acts of listening into movement and matter. Objects advanced through minute discontinuities, their apparent motion created by absences between frames. The art form therefore proved uncannily suited to Kurtág, whose music repeatedly asks the listener to construct continuity across charged gaps. Both forms make disappearance part of their syntax. The most persuasive union of image and sound came in “Ein Liebhaber der klassischen Philologie” (“A Classical Philology Aficionado”), concerning a man so enamored of Homer that he reads the German angenommen as “Agamemnon.” Books towered behind drifting clouds while statues looked on as thought acquiring mineral flesh. Beecher let the visual analog unfold slowly, giving the words time to expose the strange pathology hidden inside cultivated learning. Erudition became a benign haunting, a possession so complete that antiquity rewrote the present from within. The sequence clarified what the animations contributed to the cycle as a whole: they gave Kurtág’s microscopic dramas another surface upon which to misremember and mutate. The closing “Ein merkwürdiger Gedanke” (“A Strange Thought”) brought Kurtág’s humor to its darkest edge. Miletich and Fitz Gibbon allowed laughter to reveal its ancient kinship with fear. By then, one work had entered another through hidden roots. Cage’s knocks survived inside Kirsten’s tapping, while Beecher’s elderly voices continued inside Lichtenberg’s posthumous sentences. And through it all, Joyce’s sleeping forest returned in the Vermont woods surrounding the hall. The program cohered through subterranean recurrence, with each composition sending material below the surface for another to absorb. Marlboro’s seclusion ultimately changed the concert. Isolation became an acoustic form of relation, concentrating distant minds into one chamber. Beneath our feet, roots continued their exchanges without witnesses, each message altered by the body carrying it. The afternoon suggested that memory follows the same obscure traffic. We imagine ourselves as its custodians, although the reverse may lie closer to the truth. Memory could be the larger organism, ancient and unfinished, using each of us as a temporary organ through which to migrate. For one hour in Ragle Hall, voices became gills in that organism. The post The Forest Beneath Language: Entering the World of György Kurtág in Marlboro appeared first on Sequenza21.

items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评记述了2026年9月20日在佛蒙特州马尔伯勒音乐节Serkin中心Ragle厅上演的György Kurtág作品专场，女高音Lucy Fitz Gibbon与低音提琴手William Langlie Miletich合作演绎了为女高音与低音提琴谱写或改编的一系列作品。Kurtág的音乐以极度压缩著称，几个音便可承载完整戏剧场域的道德重量，停顿则使时间内折、孕育另一重时间。评论将马尔伯勒周围的森林与Kurtág的微观美学类比：年轮如暗语，根系延续未完之句，音乐成为语言之下那些不可见过程的听觉末梢。演出还包含Lembit Beecher为低音提琴所作的《与孙辈同行》，原为其2014年声乐套曲《观春》选段，文本素材来自多伦多与佛蒙特地区长者的访谈录音。低音泛音营造不安的摇曳感，女声则在记忆的细碎失效中探寻。遗忘与铭记被并置为同等塑造经验的力。

items.body: A saxophonist by nature, Calum Builder couldn’t help but think of the brass instrument while salvaging old church organ pipes in Northern Denmark, regarding the organ as “another aerophone working with a different kind of breath.” Honoring the prophecy of his surname, he built a reconstructed organ portable enough to take on tour. Enlisting the aid of vocalists Johanna Sulkunen and Zola Mennenöh, he combines these sounds with fragment of psalms, creating a sound that is part palimpsest, part excavation. The opening tracks are each a quarter-hour in length, allowing the listener to dive deep into the waters of divinity. “Where Can I Go” takes its lead from Psalm 139 and pairs beautifully with Andrzej Pietrewicz & Haiyue Zhu’s #10 from last year. At first there are only forlorn taps and tones, a hint of flute, a sense of desolation: hot winds blowing across even hotter sand. The darker tones come across as howls: the keening cry of the djinn. After five minutes, the harmonies emerge like an oasis, beginning the thought (“Where can I go?”) without revealing the full passage. As the vocalists sing louder and shift intonation, their repetitions become prayers. The reconstructed organ recedes, clearing space for their words to waft to the heavens. A vocal loop rides atop an organ drone, then breaks free, growing faster and more insistent. Listeners unfamiliar with the psalm may miss the underlying comfort in the unspoken words that follow, communicated only through the breath of the pipes until the closing, consoling minute. The opening timbre of “Surely” is like that of a train horn, recalling the steam engines of earlier times. One begins to muse on the similarities between instruments. Apart from being a punchline in the movie “Airplane!”, the word surely is found dozens of times in Scripture and most famously in the 23rd Psalm. Builder chooses the lesser known Psalm 139:11-12, NIV: If I say, “Surely the darkness will hide me and the light become night around me,” even the darkness will not be dark to you; the night will shine like the day, for darkness is as light to you. Behind the gorgeous vocals, a drone of darkness rises like a shroud, eclipsing but not eliminating the words. Again – as in the psalm – the overlying tone is foreboding, like an accumulated mass of daily troubles, but the underlying message is that God is still present, just as the notes remain in the pipes even after they have been removed from the church organ. The thin tendrils of sound that close the piece are like the last vestiges of night retreating from the day as the piece topples. without pause into “Is As Light.” This final movement contains some of the highest vocal notes and lowest organ notes, a contrast that underlines the theme. The album title quotes the Latin Eadem mutata resurgo, which relates not only to the logarithmic spiral, but to the nature of the soul. As famous Swiss mathematician Jakob Bernoulli writes, “The logarithmic spiral may be used as a symbol either of fortitude and consistency in adversity, or of the human body, which after all these changes, even after death, will be restored to its exact and perfect self.” Calum Builder’s album may refer more to the first, but ultimately points the way to the second. (Richard Allen)
items._genre: contemporary classical / drone / organ music / vocal experimentation
items._cn_summary: 萨克斯演奏家Calum Builder在丹麦北部回收旧教堂管风琴管道，将其重新组装为可巡演的便携式乐器，邀请人声歌手Johanna Sulkunen和Zola Mennenöh参与录制。专辑将管风琴持续音与人声片段、诗篇残篇交织，呈现出考古挖掘般的层次感。开篇两首各长达十五分钟的曲目以孤寂的音色起手，随后人声如绿洲般浮现，重复唱诵演变为祈祷；管风琴低鸣如暗夜笼罩，底层却暗示着神圣的在场。终曲以极高人声与极低管风琴形成对比，呼应专辑拉丁文标题关于灵魂与对数螺线的哲思。整体将古老宗教器物转化为当代声音艺术，融合建筑声学、人声实验与冥想性音景。

items.body: Magic Hour is both accessible and deeply experimental with its mutant ambient approach. The sonic palette employs clicks and clacks, echoes, mechanical whirs, lost terrestrial train whistles, melodic forms, shattering forms, and human murmurs, sometimes slowing or speeding up local fields to gain an emotional edge. Continuous processes of deconstruction and reconstruction Magic Hour by FeLid   Time is not a reliable empirical concept, Magic Hour combines improvisational and accidental guitar sounds, lyrical ambient drones, and high-definition sound editing. Magic Hour is both accessible and deeply experimental with its mutant ambient approach. The sonic palette employs clicks and clacks, echoes, mechanical whirs, lost terrestrial train whistles, melodic forms, shattering forms, and human murmurs, sometimes slowing or speeding up local fields to gain an emotional edge. Sharp, jarring cuts where one familiar sound instantly morphs into a new field. Drawing on all available sonic materials—including instrumental sounds, electronics, fragments of recorded audio, and environmental sounds—FeLid creates tracks and improvisational live performances through continuous processes of deconstruction and reconstruction. So many examples. Sounds with backwards envelopes, where the natural decay of a noise happens before its sharp impact. Freezing a specific moment or target in complete temporal suspension. Magic Hour is the second album by Tokyo-based artist FeLid, who combines improvisational and accidental guitar sounds, lyrical ambient drones, and high-definition sound editing. His practice is designed as a shared exploration of the relationship between sound and space, inviting audiences to experience and discover these connections together in real time. FeLid is the solo project of Kazutoshi Eguchi. He is known as a member of the post-hardcore band the north end and as a co-organizer of the festival platform MIMINOIMI. A collage of percussion instruments :: I am imagining dry mountain water, such as found in a Japanese rock garden. “Karesansui in the air #2” (5:14) opens into a collage of percussion instruments, wooden objects being tapped or struck, a curiously nourishing soup of casual fast easy flowing sounds. Here the passage of time is an objective measure. “Hello, World” (3:37) might be a welcome transparent soup of small items. Behind everything there is steamy condensation dripping and falling into a puddle on the ground, forming clusters with little gaps. Next the beat is bubbling and walking by itself, the feeling brings little scenes that open and close, and return, “Magic hour (disco)” (4:37). The ticking of the clock machinery is dark and hidden things are happening all around. The next thing I remember, I awakened in an “Environmental Mood” (3:13). We are washing stuff in the cave, bumping and scrubbing, spilling water and tossing things around, the scrubbing is the beat. Time to go to work. “Rotate Dub” (3:30) has musical lathes, a running motor sound of some kind, chattering and rattles, perhaps close views of many different motors not all at once, the power tools sing and purr. Do you feel like an afternoon rain shower? “Yuudachi Dub #2” (2:44) brings a different lathe creature here, chattering away faster, sometimes speeding like a demon, with a jittery beat, moving really quickly along, faces appear flattened in the direction they are traveling, the clock on board stretches. Our spaceship appears to move very slowly. “”Rotate Dub” (3:30) has musical lathes, a running motor sound of some kind, chattering and rattles, perhaps close views of many different motors not all at once, the power tools sing and purr. Do you feel like an afternoon rain shower?” ~Robin B. James Hold on, this next track is less than a minute in duration, “Akirame Mo Kanzin” (0:58). Metal stuff and small percussion instruments are being tapped, played backwards and forwards, very busy until the end, that occurs in an apparently irreversible succession from the past, through the present, and into the future. Now I am floating in the dark waters, “Harmonics Dub” (1:51), barely bobbing on the surface. I love the sound of guitar harmonics, textures made by energizing the strings, a mandolin being dusted off, searching for something. This turns out to lead into a haunted house, where we can play ping pong, “Sense of Gradation” (5:56) blends drone like textures with the steady ping pong tok tok tok sounds, a sound collage of real-world noises that have been warped, looped, and recontextualized into an abstract sonic experience, never busy, accenting the constant drone​ of imaginary wire strings being provoked, while the ping pong activities continue, proving the ability to use magic related to time. FeLid is also a member of MIMINOIMI, an organizing collective dedicated to exploring ambient and experimental music from multiple perspectives, and is involved in the planning and production of the urban festival Ambient / Week. Magic Hour is available on ato.archives. [Bandcamp] Magic Hour by FeLidThe post FeLid :: Magic Hour (ato.archives) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items._cn_summary: 这是东京艺术家FeLid（江口一利）的第二张专辑，以吉他即兴与偶然声响为核心素材，融合抒情氛围嗡鸣与高解析度声音编辑技术。整张作品围绕持续性的解构与重建展开：声音被加速、减速、倒转，制造出碎片化的时间感与悬停般的听觉幻觉。声响素材涵盖打击乐器拼贴、木质物体敲击、环境录音、人声呢喃以及机械嗡鸣等，形成一种介于自然与工业之间的有机质感。作品同时具备高度可听性与深度实验性，既有透明流畅的片段，也有突然的断裂与重组，邀请听者进入声音与空间关系的探索中。江口此前作为后硬核乐队成员及音乐节策展人的背景，为这张作品带来不同于常规氛围音乐的结构意识与即兴张力。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The most atypical album of David Byrne's career is also his darkest, a record where he returned to experimentation, not with world music or electronica as he had at other times, but with rock in a way he hadn't since the early days of Talking Heads. It was 1994, the era of indie and alternative rock; much had changed since 1992, the year of his previous studio album. That shift may well have influenced the group of musicians he assembled, a lineup that was anything but accidental, featuring Arto Lindsay on guitar (previously with the Lounge Lizards, John Zorn, and Marc Ribot), John Medeski on organ, Bill Ware on vibraphone (formerly of The Jazz Passengers and Groove Collective), and Bebel Gilberto, the daughter of Jo�o Gilberto."A Long Time Ago" begins to unfurl a descending, subtle mist amidst soft layers of guitar, synthesizers, and percussion, while the vocals, initially a mere whisper with a dreamlike, psychedelic quality, gradually begin to reveal their full power. Then, a sonic explosion, driven by distorted guitars and a prominent bassline, sweeps through everything in "Angels." Lyrics full of defiance and poetry, philosophical, too, delivered with deep emotion and vocal power; that vocal timbre also always held a touch of Adrian Belew, at least in its more melodic sense. And when he hit those high notes, leaving just the strumming guitar, accompanied by the bass and his voice declaring he was ready, it was a magnificent moment. It opened up from within like an explosion of light, unlike anything seen before in his career, quite the paradox for his darkest album."Crash" bursts in with a syncopated rhythm, like shattering glass; it is one of those albums where each track is sonically conceived in relation to the one preceding it, adding extra value. A dissonant guitar, paired with unconventional drumming, lends a unique touch, evoking a walk through ruins. It is as if the Smashing Pumpkins and Soundgarden were attempting a funk sound; that is how unusual the blend is, yet it succeeds brilliantly, driven by that deliberately fractured rhythm... all held together by the glue of the vocals."A Self-Made Man" has a hypnotic rhythm and a melody that gradually reveals itself to be magical and spellbinding, as he sings: "Well, I'll trade you my potential, mental illness for your bad teeth. And now we have a black market. A black market for designer genes. They've taken everything from you: the way you walk, the way you smile, the sound of your voice. I don't even know who you are. Who are you now? I am a self-made man (I have nothing left to give) I am a self-made man (I have nothing left to lose)"That is how groundbreaking this album was, and not just musically; although I like several of his solo albums, this one holds a very special place."Back In The Box" sounds modern; the guitars, featuring Arto Lindsay on the more experimental side and David Byrne on the funk side, combined with the bass and the melody in David's phrasing, create a sort of deconstructed Krautrock, albeit heavily distorted, as is the case across most of the album. The familiar Latin rhythms take on a mysterious air here, as evidenced by "Sad Song", while the energy never flags; John Medeski contributes a "gritted-teeth" rhythmic intensity that maintains its drive regardless of genre shifts."Nothing At All" reveals more of Byrne's true essence: he lays his voice bare, stretching notes to their limit amidst dissonant guitar rhythms and a sense of mystery that offers no clues as to his intentions. Only at the very end does he begin to unravel the harmonic thread, a move clearly planned from the start, concluding with instrumental codas driven by heavy cymbal work alongside distorted guitar and organ."My Love Is You" opens with bossa nova-style acoustic guitar notes, then shifts into a stark contrast to what came before, courtesy of Bill Ware. "Lilies Of The Valley" returns to playful, experimental rhythms, driven by a powerful bass and drum foundation, packed with Groove, that builds in intensity while the funk guitar seems to lock in perfectly with David. The finale is a marvelous duet between Todd Turkisher's drums and Bill Ware's vibraphone."You & Eye" keeps the syncopated funk going, with David playing the clavinet, and features a very delicate chorus that contrasts with the melody's frenetic rhythm. He hadn't lost that knack for composing songs that strike a direct chord, quite the opposite; here, there are echoes of African music in the style of Salif Keita. With Dolette McDonald on backing vocals, the same one who had worked with Sting, Stevie Winwood, and many others."Strange Ritual" is one of the key tracks, where that opening mist returns, dark and dangerous, like Naked City, while the lyrics go: "A man sits in a field, contemplating his crops. Scenes that disgust me, I see myself, I felt awe, I felt disgust, I felt bliss, I felt lust, It is not unusual, I saw people in a remote village, proudly sporting their digital watches. I saw a young Indonesian woman, possessed by the spirit of the Ninja Turtles. I saw palatial mansions with decaying decor and human furniture. I saw a legislature of women being courted by corporate lobbyists. A town whose own inhabitants do not even remember its name. We have a strange ritual. We keep it to ourselves. We are lost in love"There is a restrained violence, and gradually, in the vein of King Crimson's "Indiscipline", a section marked by calm and camouflaged rage, by a lurking violence, erupts; the vocals shift in tandem with the intensity of the music and the musicality of the words. From the mist emerges a nightmare where playing the lead role isn't frightening, because we are in control. We will never hear a more rock-oriented, fully committed David Byrne; it brings to mind King Crimson's improvisations on Starless and Bible Black. It is almost on that level."Buck Naked" is essentially just the guitar, John Medeski's organ, and David's vocals, with him giving it his all, whether in moments of presence or absence. It plays with the contrasts between calm and rage seen in his Psycho Killer era. Yet there is no nostalgia here; he breaks away from the past to launch a new phase, unafraid to keep experimenting and embracing new influences, much as he would later do with the Balanescu Quartet on 1997's Feelings. However, nowhere else is there such a sincere, honest, and unadorned outpouring of the heart as on this album, which, like the other side of a mirror, features his surname spelled in reverse.

items._cn_summary: 这张1994年的同名专辑是David Byrne职业生涯中最非典型、也最黑暗的一张作品。他回到摇滚实验的路径，组建了一支极具实验性的阵容——包括Arto Lindsay的不规则吉他、John Medeski的管风风琴、Bill Ware的颤音琴，以及Bebel Gilberto参与。专辑以层层吉他、合成器与打击乐铺陈的氛围开场，随后在《Angels》中以失真吉他与强劲贝斯线炸裂而出。《Crash》采用切分节奏与不和谐音墙，呈现出废墟般的听觉质感。《A Self-Made Man》歌词直面基因市场与身份消解的主题，旋律逐渐显露催眠般的力量。整张专辑在曲目之间形成概念性的递进关系，将放克的律动、噪音摇滚的张力与拉丁元素熔于一炉，既具有哲学深度，又在声音设计上突破预期，是Byrne个人创作序列中最具突破性的一张。

items.body: Review by Chaoticreason — 4 .5 stars.It is difficult to add any more eloquent words than Fernando has already said. It took me more than a few plays to grasp this work. That is a good thing, all too often find something immediately likeable, then wonder why I liked it a week later I hate it. However, this album has longevity, as I also believe the band has.This is a band that will stay the course, with the brilliant, and classically trained Nat Bergrin at the helm, this music is a true delight for all fans of the more progressive/experimental side of rock.Whilst I think it's fair to say that most of us love retro-sounding bands, you will only get glimpses of that from this most excellent and progressive of albums.When I first played disc, I thought "Oh wow!" a garage rock band playing very complex prog rock, which I do still stand by in some ways. But the technicality of all the players involved pushes it well beyond a garage rock band in any conventional sense. I love that they are a not a paint by numbers neo rock band. This is a band pushing musical boundaries, and I love the direction that they are taking. I love their earlier album 'Heart of a Cherry Pit Sun', but this album enters a whole new realm. This is an album well worth checking out, if your penchant is for progressive Jazz, Classical, black metal... etc. etc....In fact, if you really love the progression of progressive rock music, then this is not a band to be missed.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑被归类为RIO/Avant-Prog领域，融合了前卫爵士、古典、黑金属等多元元素，呈现出明显的实验性倾向。乐评指出作品需要多次聆听才能完全理解，这种'慢热'特性被视为优势而非缺陷，说明专辑具有持久的耐听度与深度。主创Nat Bergrin具有古典训练背景，乐手整体技术水准高超，将车库摇滚的粗糙质感与复杂的复合节拍、不谐和音程相结合，突破了常规前卫摇滚的框架。乐队拒绝成为按部就班的新摇滚团体，而是持续推进音乐边界。相比前作《Heart of a Cherry Pit Sun》，新作进入了一个全新的领域，融合了渐进爵士、古典和极端金属的影响，适合真正热爱前卫摇滚演进脉络的听众。

items.body: Band: Kraanerg | Album: Aria for Labellum Tongues | Genre: Avant-prog | Year: 2026 From: Minneapolis, USA | Label: Independent For fans of: Frank Zappa, Papangu, Sigh, Cardiacs Bandcamp Kraanerg is the brainchild of composer and multi-instrumentalist Nat Bergrin, and Aria for Labellum Tongues is their third full-length release (and their second as a full band). This was my first exposure to Kraanerg, and I was very impressed by what I encountered. Western classical music plays a massive role on this record, both in terms of instrumentation and structure. Plenty of bands will shoehorn in some violin, but not many display the ability to integrate classical influences quite like this band does. “Amargosa Raga” kicks the album off with strange, discordant guitar lines. The vocal line is surprisingly melodic for the harsh, microtonal backing, and there’s some great supporting saxophone. Classical elements play a significant role here as well, with violin and piano taking the lead on various passages. What began as a fairly harsh piece gradually evolves into a lush composition, evoking many of the Mellotron-heavy greats of the classic prog era, but run through a more modern and uncompromisingly weird lens. The title track comes next, with an onslaught of buzzy guitars, swooping strings, and tinkling vibraphone. The classical influences on this track tread a fine line between sweet and creepy, with the violin frequently adding a remorseful edge.  “Blessings in Silk, Saffron, and Naran-Ji” nearly feels like a new wave song in its opening moments. There’s a bright hopefulness, but that soon gives way to a stripped-back classical passage. Piano, violin, and scratchy clean guitar float about. The intensity of the song gradually swells with the addition of drums and wordless vocals, lifting everything upward, but with an underlying sense of tension. When rock elements eventually take the lead again, violin remains the most prominent instrument. There’s an irrepressible sense of drama, and the somewhat rough vocals feel genuinely emotional. This piece is followed by the only song under four minutes on the album, “Anguloa Virginalis (Um Rosto de Mulher)”. It’s a light and airy breather following the intensity of the previous song. Piano, vibraphone, and delicate percussion evoke loungey jazz. Gothic organ and distorted guitar kicks off “Iron Sign of the Masdevallia”. Syncopated drums and piano give this track a disorienting feel, and the dense arrangement is smothering. As the song enters an instrumental section, sax and piano both get ample time in the spotlight, each one painting a dramatic picture. Next, the song takes a surprisingly sunny turn, with piano plinking out over a (mostly) major-key backing. The guitars borrow a lot from punk, but just about everything else is more clearly indebted to classical music, which makes for an interesting contrast. This artsy punk-fusion continues as this epic enters its final few minutes. The chords become more chaotic and irregular, and the vocals become more unhinged. The music is intense, yet oddly joyous, like Cardiacs’ best work. The opening gothic passage comes back for a closing reprise, which ties things up beautifully. The album ends on its longest song, the 20-minute “Visible to the Wrong Faces”. In comparison to the storming tempo of the previous song, this one is quite restrained in its opening. Classical music predominates for the first few minutes, led by piano and saxophone. It isn’t until about four minutes in that any rock elements enter, when buzzing guitars and stomping drums begin to play supporting roles. When vocals finally enter, the music is noisy with a sense of carefully-crafted chaos. Vibraphone and violin support jangly, post-punk guitars, and the vocal melody draws from avant-garde music. Throughout this whole album, the band has shown that they are masters of textural variation and contrast, and the second half of this song is a prime example. Post-metal, classical music, and classic prog influences are all evident, and everything gels into a satisfying conclusion. Aria for Labellum Tongues is a highly ambitious and very successful musical statement. The blending of rock and classical structures is pulled off wonderfully, and each of the songs on this album feels thoughtfully put-together. It’s a long and challenging record, but it’s well worth your time. Score: 95/100

items._cn_summary: 这是一张由作曲家兼多乐器演奏者Nat Bergrin主导的前卫摇滚专辑，将西方古典音乐的结构与乐器深度融入摇滚框架，而非简单堆砌。专辑从小调微分音吉他切入，逐步演变为层次丰富的复合编曲，弦乐、钢琴、颤音琴与萨克斯交替主导段落。旋律性与不和谐音的张力持续交替，标题曲以嗡鸣吉他、低音弦乐与叮当颤音琴在甜美与不安之间游走。第三首从明亮的新浪潮式开头转入纯器乐古典段落，再缓慢积蓄张力直至摇滚段落回归，情感表达直接而强烈。短小的间奏曲目以钢琴、颤音琴与轻盈打击乐营造爵士酒廊气息。后续曲目则将哥特管风琴、朋克吉他与古典和声并置，制造出密集而失调的听感，并出人意料地转向阳光气质的大调段落。整张专辑在古典编制与摇滚能量之间频繁切换，显示出对多种风格的成熟整合能力。

items.body:
proya Plays With Ambient Music's Capacity To Comfort & Be Discomforting On EP 'Subliminal'

21 September 2026

Infusing a narrative in an ambient work, a genre often more about calm than movement by its initial design, is not a common achievement by budding artists of the genre. Therefore, it's remarkable to see Mumbai's Priya Panchwadkar aka proya manage it on her debut EP 'Subliminal'.

The wall of sound on 'find me', both placating and abrasive, echoes alongside the titular line, gradually unwinding into a tangible melodic run – something palpable finally being found from the dense cloud of sound. The metallic palette of 'INT' shifts into more botanica textures where the machine-like hiss feels more like rain before entering a more discomfortably strobing space. One shift too many for our taste, where perhaps sonic experimentation overtook compositional control, but undoubtedly creating an impressive musical world in each of its segments.

The EP title doesn't mislead, and while there are low hums that create a sense of liminal space, like on 'harvest/arriving', the producer and lens-based artist enchants the metaphorical air in those metaphorical spaces with a mix of held chords and their atonal distortions to speak more to emotions than memory of something outward. For every pleasant chime and horn line on 'snow', there is the harsh hiss and rattle of 'UGH'.

Check out the EP 'Subliminal' below and follow proya for more information.

items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”

items.body:
The brotherhood of foundational European avant garde bassists gets smaller with each passing year. And among those still living, some are either inactive for various reasons or working in other fields, musical or otherwise. So, the subset of ones still going is a small but precious list.

Among them is the Netherlands’ Arjen Gorter. Ask even a relatively informed listener of European avant garde jazz about him and almost invariably the first association will be Willem Breuker, and more specifically his Kollektief. Gorter did anchor that group for the entirety of its existence (1975-2010, with a retrospective farewell tour coming after Breuker’s death) alongside drummer Rob Verdurmen, allowing Breuker and a rotating cast of string and horn players (though trombonist Bernard Hunnekink was another stalwart) to navigate complex and subversive music, confident that a strong foundation would always support them. But like Jimmy Cobb always being referenced first and sometimes only as the last living participant of Kind of Blue after Miles Davis died in 1991, Gorter’s career, still ongoing, is hardly exclusive to his work with Breuker.

Gorter was born in Amsterdam on January 2nd, 1948 and he has resided in the Dutch capital his whole life. His road to the bass was a circuitous one. As he wrote in an email, “I liked the accordion when I was very young. It was common in the Amsterdam streets of the ‘50s, but the tunes that my teacher made me play were too silly, so that did not last. My dad imported musical instruments. He brought a slightly damaged ukulele home and so at around 11 I tried playing along with the nightly jazz broadcasts on French and Belgian radio. The father of a friend had a small jazz collection and I loved the Art Blakey Blue Note 45s, the Monk LP and the other stuff he had. So that ukulele was replaced by a guitar. I started jamming in our attic with friends and others and at some point someone brought a double bass upstairs and left it there for six months. I had fun playing it and managed to buy it from him once he showed up again.”

During high school Gorter played guitar in a band for school dances, repertoire ranging from period rock tunes to jazz compositions. He began college in 1966, aiming to study political science and sociology, the same year he first worked professionally with Breuker, having heard the older reed player’s bands around town and once playing with him at a jam session. Gorter was invited to join a new Breuker group, which performed at the Loosdrecht Jazz Competition as a sextet, then expanded to almost two-dozen musicians for the final stage. This group would make Litany for the 14th of June 1966 (Relax) in late October 1966, Gorter’s recording debut alongside two other bassists, the much older Dick van der Capellen and Victor Kaihatu.

Gorter would balance university and performing for a few years. During this time, he would work with Germany’s Gunter Hampel, appearing on his April 1968 Wergo date Gunter Hampel Group + Jeanne Lee and participating in the November 1968 Total Music Meeting in Berlin, where photo evidence has him in a bizarre encounter with Hampel, John McLaughlin, Sonny Sharrock, Pharoah Sanders, Roy Ayers, Laurie Allan, and Roel Kroes. 1969 saw even more activity: more Hampel work, including the album The 8th of July 1969 (inaugurating his Birth imprint); playing on German trumpeter Manfred Schoof’s FMP release European Echoes and being part of the Peter Brötzmann Oktett at the International Holy Hill Jazz Meeting (alongside Buschi Niebergall and Peter Kowald; Richard Williams’ review of European Echoes in the March 14th, 1970 issue of Melody Maker saying, “It’s an astonishingly powerful performance, with particularly superb work by Dudek, Bailey and the three basses, who play a really fantastic trio section.”). Gorter is also heard on the Live at The Bohemia Jazzclub recording by Hans Dulfer’s Soulbrass Inc., as well as a track with Breuker and Han and Peter Bennink heard on the Instant Composers Pool cheese box. As Gorter recalled, “I managed to juggle both activities until the end of 1969, but I was more on the road than in Amsterdam and had to make a choice and I chose the activity that gave me way more satisfaction.”

During the first half of the ‘70s, Gorter and Breuker did not work together often, at least as can be gleaned from available recordings: Hampel’s People Symphony (Birth, 1970) and part of his group that participated in German avant garde composer Hans Werner Henze’s Der Langwierige Weg In Die Wohnung Der Natascha Ungeheuer; and an unofficial Amsterdam recording from 1973 under Breuker’s leadership and a live date from Leo Cuypers in 1974, both with groups prefiguring the Kollektief (Cuypers was its first pianist). Otherwise Gorter was busy – again, at least on record – with Hans Dulfer, Kees Hazevoet, Theo Loevendie, Alexander Von Schlippenbach, and the Irène Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl Quartet. The latter two were significant. Gorter was part of the second iteration of Schlippenbach’s Globe Unity Orchestra, Niebergall and Kowald in tow once more (a 1970 Berlin Jazz Festival performance released in 2001) and the Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl group that was active for several years. “I met Rudiger in Wuppertal, that was a new jazz center by itself thanks to Peter Brötzmann and Peter Kowald,” wrote Gorter. “Sometimes I stayed at the studio that he shared with guitar wizard Hans Reichel. When Irene and Rudiger started playing together, they asked me to join and we played many places in the early ‘70s, with Heinrich Hock, Louis Moholo, or Alan Bateman on drums.” That band made only one full album, 1974’s Goose Pannée (FMP) but did have a track on the For Example - Workshop Freie Musik 1969 - 1978, the FMP boxed set.

1974-75 was an important period for two other reasons. Besides the aforementioned collaborations as well as work with the Boy Edgar Big Band and the small groups of Maurice Horsthuis and Toon van Vliet, Gorter was one of the musicians who helped establish Amsterdam’s Bimhuis, ultimately one of Europe’s premier venues for avant garde music, performing on its October 1st, 1974 opening night with the Burton Greene Quartet. Then in March 1975, Breuker asked Gorter to be a member of his Kollektief. Gorter described the group’s music as such: “Willem’s music had a lot of freedom. There were often tightly arranged written sections that would suddenly end and then the fun was to play on as if the arrangement continued – there was usually no such thing as chord changes – or to let the thing fall off a cliff ... Anyway, the music always felt fresh to play, even after many concerts, and there was a great mix of individual input and group discipline and cooperation. The Kollektief’s music linked the recognizable to the unexpected, often in 90-degree turns. It was surprising but accessible. For us musicians there was a wide spectrum of activities, from theater plays to movie music to interpretations of classical music and a lot of traveling to places where we found appreciative audiences, ranging from Australian school children to Chinese businessmen.”

The Kollektief would go on to make over three dozen albums, mostly released on Breuker’s BV Haast label, and perform all over the world, including during the Klap op de Vuurpijl (roughly, Top It All Off) Festival, taking place over five days at the end of each year from 1976-2005. Its book mixed Breuker and other band member pieces with tunes from various pages of the Great American Songbook and drawn from the classical canon, as well as other sources, presented in a highly theatrical manner best appreciated live and mixing in humor in refreshing contrast to the dour stage demeanor of many an improviser.

As busy as the Kollektief would keep him, Gorter still pursued other projects, some including fellow Kollektief members, including Breuker, and only existing on stages, such as groups under the leadership of Maarten van Norden, Sean Bergin, Boy Raaymakers, Pierre Courbois, Nedly Elstak, Jasper van ‘t Hof, Misha Mengelberg, and others. A representative sampling of those can be found in the archive of the Bimhuis (https://www.bimhuis.nl/archief); when he was in Amsterdam, this would be Gorter’s home near his home.

But there were also ones documented as albums: Maine, the 1975 collaboration of American trombonist Roswell Rudd with Dulfer, Gorter, and drummer Martin van Duynhoven, was made up of music by Sonny Rollins and Rudd (who had been coming to and working in the Netherlands since the mid ‘60s both with the New York Art Quartet and also locals like Loevendie). There were two 1977 dates by Cuypers, Zeeland Suite also including another bassist in South African expatriate Harry Miller; the 1979 Maarten Van Norden/Boy Raaymakers quartet date Chicken Song, completed by drummer Peter Nykyruj (of Mike Osborne fame); and a pair of 1980 albums spearheaded by the aforementioned trumpeter/composer Elstak (and released on his Coreco label; Gorter had loosely studied harmony with him in the ‘60s): To Build was led by Soesja Citroen’s name, who was one of five singers alongside Elstak, Breuker, Gorter, and Van Duynhoven for Sad Trumpets. The most significant, at least in terms of international exposure, came in July 1984, when Gorter, Mengelberg, and Bennink joined forces with two Americans, soprano saxophonist Steve Lacy and trombonist George Lewis, for the Soul Note release Change of Season (Music Of Herbie Nichols). Another important recording came 13 years later with Legendary: The 27th of May 1997, in a reunion with Hampel, who was fêting his seminal Heartplants SABA album from 1965 with original participants Courbois, Schlippenbach, and Schoof, Gorter standing in for his late friend Buschi Niebergall. One interesting takeaway from this is that it is often thought that after Breuker split with his fellow Instant Composers Pool founders Mengelberg and Bennink there were two distinct worlds in Dutch avant garde jazz; however, there were musicians like Gorter who operated in both spheres.

The new millennium found Gorter in several new projects: the mostly American blues/jazz band New Texas Swing from American saxophonist and then fellow Kollektief member Alex Coke with singer Tina Marsh and drummer John Betsch; the aptly named though horn-heavy Drummers Double Bill from Arend Niks and Verdurmen; 2000 recording The Compositions Of Eric Dolphy (BV Haast) with Coke, Breuker, Eric Vloeimans, Frank van Bommel, and John Engels; and Bo Van De Graaf’s I Compani; and the Rahsaan Roland Kirk “tribute” band Reeds & Deeds, also put together by Van De Graaf.

The Dolphy project had a personal resonance for Gorter, more specifically a much younger version of himself. In 1964, when he was 16, Gorter attended the Charles Mingus Sextet performance at Amsterdam’s Concertgebouw, a band with Dolphy, Johnny Coles, Clifford Jordan, Jaki Byard, and Dannie Richmond, which Gorter calls “the best ever ... Halfway through a trumpet solo by Johnny Coles, Eric left the stage while playing and walked into the hall. He ended up right next to my seat, way in the back. For a 16-year-old, that may have been a life-changing experience.” In 2011, Gorter was given the opportunity to celebrate Dolphy once more with a concert at the Bimhuis: “Eric Dolphy at The Five Spot Revisited,” with the legendary recording’s repertoire played by himself, Tom Arthurs, Rudi Mahall/Alex Coke (as his bass clarinet and saxophone/flute sides), Benoît Delbecq, and John Betsch.

Gorter joined the multimedia ensemble I Compani, founded by Van De Graaf in 1985, in 2010. As he wrote, “Bo van de Graaf just called it quits for I Compani, which I understand but regret. He led that band for 40 years through great adventures and I was happy to participate since 2010 or so. If anyone is comparable to Breuker in the amount of initiatives he took, it is him. Original pieces are blended with film music and live video, in various lineups from septet to 18-piece band. His music has the space, freedom and versatility of Breuker’s, but in a different way. Fun!”

When asked about the European scene in which he came up, Gorter replied, “At that time every European city had a very original and recognizable improvised music scene, or a few of them, like London with both the Spontaneous Music Ensemble and Brotherhood of Breath,” he wrote. “And they all had international contacts and were sharing with each other. So, the originality of these approaches, and the mutual respect, encouraged the exchange between countries and scenes and the musicians and their supporters took the initiative to made it happen.”

As for his own methodology towards, as shown in this piece, the variety of musical situations in which he has taken part, Gorter spoke both simply and profoundly: “From the beginning I played both free improvisation and tunes based on chord changes. Learning on stage was an option in the ‘60s, which sometimes led to embarrassment but more often to improvement. My approach is: first try to play what you hear, then figure out what others call it (= music theory), then apply that to play better what you hear and so on. Nowadays much education starts on the second step ...”

items._cn_summary: 本文聚焦荷兰低音提琴手Arjen Gorter的职业生涯，从早年玩手风琴与尤克里里的经历讲起，详述他如何从政治学学生逐步走上爵士乐道路。文章重点回顾了他1966年与Willem Breuker的合作起点，包括在Loosdrecht爵士比赛中的亮相以及首张录音Litany for the 14th of June 1966的诞生过程。文中指出Gorter长期作为Breuker Kollektief的核心节奏支柱，与鼓手Rob Verdurmen一同支撑起Breuker复杂而颠覆性的音乐构想，同时也强调了他个人音乐身份的独立性，不应被简单视为Breuker的附属。文章还提及他与德国多乐器演奏家Gunter Hampel的合作录音，展现其在欧洲前卫爵士圈中的广泛参与。整体行文兼具史料梳理与人物特写性质。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.

items._genre: avant-garde / experimental / ambient / contemporary classical / protest folk
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是多萝西·莫斯科维茨与意大利作曲家弗朗西斯科·保罗·帕拉迪诺、诗人卢卡·奇诺·法拉利合作的《慈悲之歌》。音乐以钢琴为核心，叠加弦乐、木管与合成器织体，刻意回避传统功能和声进行，采用模态与非线性结构，呈现类似史蒂夫·赖克与菲利普·格拉斯的简约重复美学。人声部分延续1960年代抗议歌曲传统，歌词直面当代议题，从白人至上主义与极权主义威胁到对死亡与宇宙位置的沉思。莫斯科维茨的演唱方式介于叙事与意识流之间，钢琴则像古希腊合唱队般在旁评论。专辑将实验器乐写作与政治诗性歌词融为一体，既是对当下分裂时刻的回应，也是对六十年代反文化音乐遗产的延续与重构。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 乐队的这张专辑以自制的非常规乐器为核心卖点，乐手们用废旧物品手工打造了低音号、厨房号、坚果单簧管等怪诞乐器，并在现代录音环境下呈现出精准的音准和饱满的音质。专辑将克雷兹默、昆比亚、桑巴、非洲节拍与中东旋律等多种世界音乐传统杂糅一体：开篇的克雷兹默曲调用夸张的单簧管与巴松管制造狂欢感，昆比亚段落则交由特色长笛与拉丁打击乐主导，非洲节拍段落布满木鱼、摇铃与马林巴琴的层次。各曲保留了大量的即兴段落，乐手在节奏之上展开爵士化的炫技对位。整张专辑既是对世界音乐多样性的礼赞，也以废物利用的DIY精神呼应了音乐本质中跨越文化与器材的创造力。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.
