items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家 Omar Sosa 在意大利 Fazioli 钢琴厂的音乐厅中进行两小时无脚本独奏即兴，录音后通过混音叠加人声采样、打击乐、循环音段、田野录音与环境声响。整张专辑延续其跨越爵士、拉丁、非洲与世界音乐的融合风格，Sosa 明确表示拒绝被归类为任何特定流派，秉持"少即是多"的美学，强调即兴首遍录制的自然表达。专辑标题《Sendas》（路径）呼应其音乐哲学：在传统根基上持续演化，探索低频脉轮共鸣般具有精神性的声音层次。制作上结合现场即兴与后期实验性拼贴，展现了独立艺术家的创作自由度。

items.body: Tony Njoku‘s recent work has moved between open-ended instrumental composition and song. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE continues this movement in a more intimate setting. Across four pieces, piano, synthesisers and space provide the foundations of the music. The title track establishes the EP’s sound through layers of synthesiser harmonies that gather pace but stop short of a conventional climax. “Streams and Storms” turns towards private reflection, while “The Quiet Chaos of Playing It Safe” holds onto its tension without seeking a dramatic release. “Etude No. 1” strips the music down again, bringing the record to a sombre close. As Njoku explains in the accompanying interview, his move away from language is connected to an interest in how music can communicate feelings before they have been organised into words. Grief, exhaustion and recovery remain unresolved, expressed through harmony, resonance, dynamics and space. Small harmonic changes assume greater significance within these sparse arrangements. This is no suite in four movements, with constrasting character and same key signature. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE is a protean EP that searches and digs inwards, taking unexpected turns without any desire to dazzle. There is no show-off moment, no virtuoso display demanding attention, nor any grand moment of portending grief; emotion remains understated and kept in check. The music is unafraid of intimacy, allowing sustained harmonies, shifts in density and silence to determine its course, leaving much of the experience behind these compositions unspoken. To help us put out the fire we reached out directly to Tony Njoku for an interview conducted via email. All Our Knives Are Always Sharp was a large-scale collaborative statement concerned with spiritual preparedness, cultural resistance and collective survival, while the Bloom releases increasingly embraced instrumental composition, chamber arrangements and themes of grief, memory and renewal. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE feels like a further step in that direction: intensely personal, largely wordless and driven by the need to work through difficult emotions rather than narrative. Do you see this EP as the culmination of a journey that began with those recent releases, or did it emerge from a fundamentally different place? I don’t think of it as a culmination so much as another point of arrival. Each project tends to emerge from whatever questions I’m living with at the time. All Our Knives… was very outward-facing. It was about community, about bringing different voices into conversation around ideas of resilience and collective memory. Bloom and the instrumental work that followed became quieter spaces where I could sit with loss, change and the slower work of transformation. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE came from an even more internal place. I wasn’t trying to tell a story or resolve anything. I was more interested in documenting a state of being and exorcising some pent-up feelings that were essentially causing me harm. The music became a way of staying present with difficult emotions rather than translating them into language. In that sense it feels connected to the recent releases, but I wasn’t consciously trying to complete a trilogy or close a chapter. It simply became the form those experiences needed. One of the recurring threads across recent works—from The Loops (Grief) and Looking For Light to the standalone single “Malaise”—is an engagement with emotional turbulence that is neither entirely despairing nor entirely hopeful. The title track of A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE speaks of moving through fire rather than escaping it. Has your understanding of grief, burnout and recovery changed over the course of these releases, and do you think this EP arrives at a different emotional destination than those earlier works? I think grief has become less about something to overcome and more about something you learn to live alongside. Earlier work probably carried a stronger desire to find resolution or to move towards the light. I don’t think I see it that way anymore. Recovery isn’t linear, and neither is burnout. There are moments of joy inside exhaustion and moments of uncertainty inside healing. The image of moving through fire rather than escaping it felt important because some experiences can’t be bypassed. They change you. The music on this EP isn’t trying to extinguish the fire; it’s trying to understand what remains after you’ve passed through it. If there’s hope here, it’s a quieter kind. It’s found in endurance, attention and the possibility of continuing to create despite everything. One of the striking aspects of All Our Knives Are Always Sharp was the way you brought together an extraordinary community of Black British voices—Tricky, GAIKA, Ghostpoet, Coby Sey, James Massiah, Space Afrika, Labi Junior and others—creating a record that felt simultaneously personal and collective. More broadly, your recent work has moved freely between songs, spoken-word collaborations, chamber-like compositions, ambient electronics and abstract instrumental forms. By contrast, A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE feels almost entirely self-contained, built around piano, synthesisers and extended instrumental pieces. After such a collaborative album, did the absence of other voices create a different kind of honesty or vulnerability? Collaboration has always been fundamental to my practice because it allows ideas to exist beyond my own perspective. All Our Knives… couldn’t have existed without those voices. The conversations between people were the point of the record. With this EP I found myself needing the opposite experience. I needed solitude, not because I wanted to withdraw from community, but because I needed to hear what was underneath all the noise. Working mostly alone meant there was nowhere to hide. Every hesitation, every silence, every decision belonged to me. That can feel vulnerable, but it can also be very freeing because you’re no longer trying to explain yourself through words or through other people’s interpretations. I also needed space to cry and I find that’s a hard thing for me to do in front of people, I let go of my masks the most in solitude. So it became a conversation with the instruments themselves. The piano, synthesizers and space all became collaborators in a different sense. You’ve described this EP as a collection of “raging exhalations, quiet revelations, subtle smirks of humility, laments and meditations.” Unlike many of your previous releases, there are no guest vocalists, no lyrics and no obvious narrative anchors. Did working without words feel liberating or exposing? And at this stage in your career, do you feel instrumental music has become just as capable as song of carrying the political, spiritual and emotional concerns that have always been central to your work? Working without words was both liberating and exposing. Lyrics can sometimes direct people towards a particular meaning, whereas instrumental music leaves much more room for the listener’s own experience. That openness was something I wanted to embrace. I’ve become increasingly interested in what music communicates before language enters. Breath, texture, resonance, silence… these things carry meaning too. They can hold emotion in ways that words sometimes can’t. I don’t really separate instrumental music from song anymore. They’re just different ways of asking the same questions. The political, spiritual and emotional concerns that have always interested me don’t disappear when language disappears. They become embodied differently. Sometimes a sustained note or a shift in harmony can express something that would become smaller if I tried to explain it. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: Tony Njoku 这张 EP 由四首作品构成，以钢琴、合成器与空间感为核心，呈现出向器乐创作倾斜的轨迹。标题曲通过合成器和声的层层堆叠逐步推进，却在接近高潮时收住；后续曲目分别朝向内省、压抑张力与极简收束展开，整体拒绝戏剧性释放，转而依靠和声变化、密度位移与留白来传达悲伤、疲惫与恢复等难以言说的情感。Njoku 本人在访谈中表示，这张作品源自更私密的内心状态，不再追求叙事或结论，而是对某种存在状态的记录与释放。整体而言，音乐在克制中保持亲密感，适合在安静环境下反复聆听。

items.body: German medieval techno act Klangschmiede & Friends released the single “Remember” on September 1, 2026, and submitted it as an application for Germany’s national selection process for the Eurovision Song Contest 2027. The full application was uploaded to public broadcaster SWR on the same day; German participation in the 2027 contest is not yet confirmed. Live bagpipes, hurdy-gurdy and flute sit alongside electronic production on “Remember,” with English lyrics and passages in Old High German drawn from early medieval sources such as the Hildebrandslied. The track runs just under three minutes and moves between medieval techno, dark electronic production and historical folk balladry. Klangschmiede & Friends’ Eurovision 2027 bid For the submission, Klangschmiede expanded into the extended line-up Klangschmiede & Friends, bringing in additional musicians for the song’s acoustic instrumentation. The official music video was filmed with the full ensemble at Schloss Burg in Solingen on August 17, 2026. Regional public broadcaster WDR was on site for the shoot and aired a television feature on the production through its Lokalzeit Bergisches Land program. The submission has also drawn coverage from ESC kompakt and regional newspapers including the Solinger Tageblatt and the Remscheider General-Anzeiger. About Klangschmiede Klangschmiede is the duo of Claudia Sokoll and Timo Tofaute, based in the Bergisches Land region of Germany and operating officially since 2025. The project mixes medieval and Nordic folk elements with electronic production, drawing on historical sources such as the Hildebrandslied, the Poetic Edda and Nordic ballads. Its catalog includes the album “RITUS”, released digitally and on CD on May 14, 2026, and singles including “Nothing We Love Is Ever Gone” (March 26, 2026), “Hüter der Straße” (April 30, 2026) and “Solringen” (July 23, 2026), alongside a remix of “Tanz den Feuertanz” featuring Keltania. Klangschmiede has also worked with the medieval folk-rock band Corvus Corax on the track “Ragnarök”. “Remember”, released as a single on September 1, 2026 under the expanded name Klangschmiede & Friends, is the project’s submission for Germany’s national Eurovision Song Contest 2027 selection, with participation still to be confirmed.

items._cn_summary: 这是一篇关于德国二人组 Klangschmiede 提交作品参与 2027 年欧洲电视歌唱大赛德国选拔的新闻报道。其单曲《Remember》将活体风笛、手摇风琴与长笛等中世纪乐器与电子制作结合，歌词混合英语与古高地德语，取材自《希尔德布兰特之歌》等早期中世纪文本。音乐在'中世纪 techno'、暗潮电子与历史民谣叙事之间切换，时长不足三分钟，结构紧凑。为此次参赛，组合扩展为 Klangschmiede & Friends 阵容，MV 在索林根的布格城堡拍摄。作品同时呈现北欧民谣元素，融合《诗歌埃达》及北欧叙事曲素材，此前还与中世纪民谣摇滚乐队 Corvus Corax 合作过曲目。该项目立足于贝吉施地区，自 2025 年正式运作，作品以独立与小规模区域媒体曝光为主，带有鲜明的德国地方文化视角与中世纪文本的历史纵深感。

items.body: The Sound Veil Society‘s debut album “Things We Kept” is built around an unusual kind of intensity. The record rarely reaches for aggression or dramatic excess; instead, emotional weight accumulates through restraint, space, repetition and the careful relationship between voice, electronics and silence. That became even clearer to me after seeing the duo at E-Only before spending more time with the album. Live, the songs seemed capable of becoming physically larger without sacrificing the intimacy they carry on record. The Swedish-Norwegian project brings together Erlend Eilertsen and Hans-Olof Mattsson, two musicians with extensive histories in Nordic electronic music, but “Things We Kept” does not sound like an exercise in accumulated experience or genre expertise. The more interesting question is what happens when experience becomes instinct: when musicians know enough to stop demonstrating what they know and instead concentrate on what a song actually needs. Released on 11 September 2026 through Progress Productions, “Things We Kept” is the duo’s first full-length album. Its title becomes more revealing as the record unfolds. What we keep is not necessarily what we consciously choose to preserve. Memory, grief, unfinished conversations, attachments and previous versions of ourselves remain present long after circumstances have changed. That tension between movement and emotional permanence runs quietly through an album whose apparent delicacy repeatedly turns out to carry considerable force. The Sound Veil Society interview Karo: I saw you at E-Only before hearing “Things We Kept”, and what struck me was that the performance generated enormous emotional pressure without relying on aggression or theatrical excess. Is restraint something you consciously build into The Sound Veil Society, or is it simply where the two of you naturally meet? The Sound Veil Society: It’s the natural way for us to express ourselves, and TSVS is the outlet where we can give these feelings and emotions free space in our performance, both on record and live. Karo: “Things We Kept” is a debut album made by musicians who are anything but beginners. Does starting a new project after years of experience give you greater freedom, or does experience make it harder to surprise yourselves because you already know too well what works? The Sound Veil Society: Good question! In a way, it gives us more freedom, as we use our experience together with what we have learned over the years to create something new. But it might just be the circle of life, as we evolve through different phases in our lives, with new experiences and so on. And it would be boring to repeat ourselves, so to trigger creativity and motivation, we just do what we like and hopefully someone else likes it as well. Karo: The album feels remarkably coherent across music, lyrics, photography, videos and the physical booklet. Did you think of “Things We Kept” as a complete world from the beginning, or did that visual and emotional language gradually reveal itself while the music was taking shape? The Sound Veil Society: We did have an idea from the beginning to be very visual in what we do as TSVS. The album itself is a result of our journey in making it. After a year or so of making a lot of demos, we decided where we wanted to take our sound, and after that everything just fell into place. “Things We Kept” became a complete world through the process and, indeed, there is a thought behind the booklet, videos and music completing each other. Karo: There is something almost paradoxical about this record: it sounds delicate, but never weak. I kept thinking of tempered glass: transparent, apparently fragile, yet internally capable of carrying enormous force. Where does that balance between vulnerability and strength come from in your writing? The Sound Veil Society: Really like your reflection of the record! It reflects quite well who we are as people, in a way, as both of us are emotional beings, with our share of struggles both in the past and present. But that can also be used as a strength, because you need a certain amount of strength to deal with the challenges in life. So for us it is a very natural process and nothing we “try” to do. It just happens that way. Karo: The lyrics repeatedly return to movement: leaving, running, waiting, returning, searching for air. Yet emotionally, many of the characters seem unable to escape what they carry with them. Were you consciously interested in the difference between physically moving on and actually changing? The Sound Veil Society: Not really. It is just our way of describing thoughts and feelings that are close to us, or stories and reflections that have inspired us over the years. Karo: The title “Things We Kept” becomes more interesting the longer one spends with the record, because what people keep is often not something they would consciously choose: grief, unfinished conversations, versions of other people, even destructive attachments. What does “keeping” mean to you in the context of this album? The Sound Veil Society: We think that everything we experience, be it good or bad, stays with us to some degree, even when we have almost forgotten about it, because it shapes us into who we are right now. Without all the experiences we go through in life, we would not be the same people we are today. Karo: Erlend’s voice is very exposed in these songs, but the arrangements rarely try to underline every emotion he expresses. How do you decide when the music should support the voice and when it should deliberately leave it almost alone? The Sound Veil Society: It’s all about the feeling, really, and nothing we think too much about when we make music. To express ourselves the way we want, it just tends to become like that. Karo: One thing I noticed both at E-Only and on the album is how important space is. The songs are not afraid of air, pauses or sounds that are allowed to remain isolated. In electronic music, where it is technically very easy to keep adding layers, is knowing what to remove as important to you as knowing what to write? The Sound Veil Society: In a way it is, but the most important thing for us is to write a good song and express the feeling we want to express with it. We do use quite a lot of layers, but they are often subtle and just there to emphasise the sound. Since we have some years behind us making music, we have learned that sometimes less is more. Karo: The visual material often uses roads, water, landscapes, silhouettes and people partly disappearing from view. They feel less like illustrations of individual songs than fragments of memory. How closely do you work on the relationship between image and sound, and what can an image express that you deliberately leave unresolved in the lyrics? The Sound Veil Society: It depends on the idea of the song we are working on, but we often get visual ideas while making music. An image or a video clip itself is a great way to describe emotions, and combining sound and visuals simply makes a story more complete. Karo: Your musical backgrounds give you access to an established electronic vocabulary, yet “Things We Kept” does not sound interested in demonstrating genre knowledge. Was there anything from your previous projects that you consciously had to unlearn in order for The Sound Veil Society to develop its own identity? The Sound Veil Society: Not much, really. The only thing we have been trying to do is shorten parts, as it is easy to keep things simply because they sound good, but in the end they often just make a track less interesting. Other than that, everything else just fell into place during the making of it. Karo: At E-Only I had the impression that some of these songs actually became larger through performance without losing their intimacy. Has playing the material in front of people changed your understanding of the album, perhaps shown you emotional qualities in certain songs that were less obvious in the studio? The Sound Veil Society: It can happen, but we often already have an idea of how a song will work live when we make it. So most of our work is made just as much for the live stage as it is for a record, actually. Of course, before the first live show, we didn’t know how our vision would translate to the audience, but after these shows we really feel that we get a special connection with the audience. Karo: “Things We Kept” establishes a very precise emotional and visual identity for a first album. Looking ahead, does that identity now feel like a foundation you want to deepen, or something you already feel tempted to disturb? What are you curious to discover about The Sound Veil Society next? The Sound Veil Society: In a way, it is a foundation to build upon and is, in many ways, the core of our concept. But we do want to evolve and make something new along the way, so we don’t yet know what it will become. But that is also part of the fun: exploring new sides of a concept. We will always aim to be as honest and raw in our expression. About The Sound Veil Society The Sound Veil Society is a Swedish-Norwegian electronic duo formed in 2024 by Erlend Eilertsen and Hans-Olof Mattsson. Eilertsen is associated with Essence Of Mind and Lights A.M. and joined Xenturion Prime in 2024; Mattsson co-founded Code 64, later established Xenturion Prime and has also been involved with Essence Of Mind. The project debuted with “The River” on 24 April 2025, followed by “OK” on 22 August 2025 and “Hunger for Light” in March 2026. Their debut album, “Things We Kept”, was released by Progress Productions on 11 September 2026. The standard edition contains eleven tracks, including “Voices” featuring KÅRP; the CD adds three bonus versions, while the album was also issued on black-and-white splatter vinyl and as a limited MiniDisc edition. The duo performed at Nocturnal Culture Night and E-Only Festival; a live video for “Nothing to Say” was recorded at E-Only in Leipzig in March 2026. The Sound Veil Society are already confirmed for Eastside Festival in Halle (Saale), Germany, on 2-3 July 2027.

items._cn_summary: The Sound Veil Society的首张专辑《Things We Wept》以克制为核心美学，通过留白、重复与人声与电子之间的微妙关系积累情感重量。两位北欧音乐人Erlend Eilertsen与Hans-Olof Mattsson将丰富的电子音乐经验转化为本能，不再炫耀技术，而是让歌曲本身说话。专辑探讨记忆、悲伤、未完成的对话与旧日自我的持续存在，表面细腻的质地暗藏巨大力量。采访揭示了创作中的自然表达与自我进化的理念，乐队强调将经验转化为自由的创作空间。这是一张在Progress Productions厂牌下发行的北欧电子作品，融合了暗潮的氛围质感与极简主义的情感表达。

items.body: Purest Form Resistance Dais Records Despite its brief fifteen minute runtime, there’s a meal to be made out of LA trio Purest Form’s latest EP, their debut on Dais, both in terms of attitude and presentation, as well as what its selection of very clear influences might portend for the larger post-industrial landscape. Drawing upon familiar markers of 90s electronic aggression, Resistance provides a tight test case for their read on that historical moment. Opener “Animal” functions as a strong calling card for Purest Form, showing both their capacity for a catchy, heavily processed guitar riff as well as Story Beeson’s acidic growl that’s part grindcore, part death metal. Factor in just the right amount of backing programming and an easily chantable chorus and it becomes both cathartic and anthemic in short order. It is, to be glib, exactly the type of thrashing industrial rock glory which KMFDM have been failing to recapture for the past couple of decades. Much of the rest of the EP’s made up of densely programmed two-minute wipeouts jammed up with breaks, more heavily processed guitar now functioning more for colour than riffs, and more spleen and vile being vented. If that sounds on paper fairly akin to digital hardcore, listening to “Break” and “More” will do little to dissuade that presumption. “Beyond Terror” acts as a quick riposte to this frenetic pace, offering post-hardcore chug while the vocals cut through equivocations about the killings of Palestinians – “call it what you like, it’s genocide.” And then there’s the closing cover. Fifteen or twenty years back, an industrial metal act doing a straightforward version of The Prodigy’s “Breathe” would have felt awkwardly retrograde. However, a full three decades on from the original release and overdriven into the red to the point that it’s difficult to distinguish original tracks from sampled ones, Purest Form’s take on “Breathe” feels like the best sort of “oh shit, they’re covering this?” moment at the end of a packed and sweaty basement show. In discussing the appeal of the 90s sources Pures Form borrow from it’s important to not overstate how new they might be to the band; both Beeson and guitarist/programmer Madi Woodward both have lengthy rap sheets with slews of hardcore and metal acts going back a decade or so. But there’s no question that a combination of their backgrounds beyond industrial and the historical space separating Resistance from those acts helps invigorate their dense and furious angle on them. Buy it. RESISTANCE by PUREST FORM The post Purest Form, “Resistance” appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items._cn_summary: 洛杉矶三人组 Purest Form 的首张 Dais 厂牌 EP 仅十五分钟，却以密集的编程、过度处理的吉他 riff 和 grindcore 嗓音浓缩了九十年代电子攻击性的核心语汇。开场曲"Animal"展示强烈的工业摇滚气质，被乐评比作 KMFDM 近年未能复现的辉煌；中段曲目如"Break"和"More"以两分钟左右的密集结构推进，接近 digital hardcore 的暴力美学；"Beyond Terror"则放慢节奏转向 post-hardcore 切分，歌词直指巴勒斯坦议题并明确称之为种族灭绝。尾声翻唱 The Prodigy 的"Breathe"，将原曲推至过载极限，模糊采样与原始音轨的边界，呈现出地下室演出般的粗粝能量。乐队成员此前活跃于硬核与金属场景，跨界背景赋予了这张作品对九十年代素材的鲜活诠释。

items.body: " All Art Has Been Contemporary ” This sentence is a neon installation by conceptual artist Maurizio Nannucci located on the roof of the Galleria d'Arte Moderna in Torino, that takes up a similar concept expressed a few decades earlier by Pablo Picasso. Such a fundamental axiom, around which rivers of ink have been spilled, seems to lose its actualization in the late '70s, early '80s, with regard to jazz: this art form is out of sync with the “here and now” and doesn't dialogue with contemporary, ontologically expressed by young generations. Totally deprived of any chance to become aware of free/improv artists, the teens of the time (your humble writer among them) relate to jazz in the same way they approach Dante, Seneca or Milton in highschool or uni: respect, awe, in some cases sincere passion, more often distance. Wright or wrong, a matter of fact. Moreover, those years were destined to write one of the brightest chapters in the Great Book of Music, through amazing groups like Clock DVA, PIL, Joy Division, Talking Heads, Pere Ubu, X, Television, Bad Brains, Wire, just to throw out some names in bulk. Would it have made sense to spend the very little bucks in our pocket on Chet Baker instead of Meat Puppets and Husker Du? C’mon, a no-brainer. This inexhaustible cornucopia of punk/post-punk gems experiences a small, apparently insignificant, intermittence, which leads us, aboard the only ISO-certified Time Machine (the music), to where almost everything happens: New York. Here, while the ruins of CBGB's and Max's Kansas City are still smoking, a patrol of sappers (Contortions, Mars, DNA, Teenage Jesus and the Jerks), pushing far beyond punk, lights up the charges of the “No Wave”, generating a shockwave that transcends the scope of music and involves the most extremist artistic fringes of the East Village and the Lower East Side: poets (Lydia Lunch), writers (Kathy Acker), painters (Basquiat) and filmmakers (Eric Mitchell, Amos Poe) are up for It. Among them, relocated from Minnesota, John Lurie, iconic muse actor from Jim Jarmusch’s early movies, who in his unmissable autobiography, The History of Bones , offers us a snapshot of that sparkling, bohemian milieu: “We were so sure of ourselves, we never doubted anything. We were powerful, intelligent, energetic, confident, self-centered, and incredibly naive. Nothing outside our fourteen-block radius mattered. From Houston to 14th St., from the Bowery to Ave. A, that was the only universe.” John alternates between filmmaking and musical practicing, not on a third-hand Telecaster or on a battered Precision bass, but on alto saxophone: "At 4 p.m. on Main Street in Worcester, Massachusetts, the universe gave me my first saxophone. Nothing special happened, except that a man, driving around with a wheelbarrow, gave me a saxophone. I became like a monk. I slept on the floor, I didn't have a TV, I didn't smoke, I didn't drink, I didn't fuck. I played the saxophone until my fingers bled and I devoured music: Varese, Stravinsky, Mingus, Dolphy, Monk, Bird, Ornette, Hendrix." From there, it was a short step to form a band, and with his brother Evan on keyboards, the rhythm section of Steve Piccolo and Anton Fier (of Feelies “fame”), and the abrasive guitar of DNA’s Arto Lindsay (a very distinctive element of the ensemble), the Lounge Lizards were born, self-described, out of respect for the Masters of the Past, as "fake jazz." The Purists, losers by definition, take the bait and move on, while those with heart and soul stop, listen to and understand the new hybridization of tradition with the metro, iconoclastic, infectious, no-sounds: a sabotage of the “status quo ante” of jazz but, definitively, a Sabotage of Love. None of them graduated from Juilliard (does it matter?), but the Lizards' sound reflects like few others the zeitgeist of Downtown and the mood of those courageous and visionary prime movers who animate it. Their debut album was released in 1981, packaged with Peter Saville's splendid artwork, featuring a black-and-white photo of the musicians on the cover that always reminds us of Jimmy Giuffre's stunning "Free Fall". At the helm, the mighty Teo Macero who infuses the album with the nocturnal atmospheres that made it legendary, sitting the listener at the bar counter of Edward Hopper's "Nighthawks At Diner" or amidst a Raymond Chandler novel. The quick band’s development during the couple of years preceding it is captured on "Live 79-81," a reissue of the 1985 Roir cassette, containing live recordings at Hurrah and CBGB's in New York (June, August 1979), Her Majesty's Theater in London (June 1980), Cleveland Radio (June 1981), and Berlin Jazz Festival (December 1981). It's all there: contractions and swing, dissonances and post-post-bop, Earl Hagan (Harlem Nocturne) and Monk (Epistrophy), boredom and coolness, dark streets and streetlights. Jazz in its pure form. Did Lounge Lizards change the course of events? No. Did they spearhead a new musical stream? No. Did they contribute to ensuring that kids who grew up on punk could relate to jazz in an updated and conscious way? ABSOLUTELY YES. Same as it happened to John Lurie just some years before, then let him have the final words to come full circle: “When I was 17, someone made me listen to John Coltrane and it was as if he was speaking to me in Chinese. But how? Is there music I can't understand? And so I started listening to it all the time.” Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 本文以艺术概念开篇，串联七十年代末至八十年代初纽约下城文化生态。文章并非聚焦专辑音乐本体，而是将 Lounge Lizards 置于 CBGB 衰败后 No Wave 浪潮的语境中铺陈历史：Contortions、DNA、Teenage Jesus and the Jerks 等乐队将朋克推至极端，与诗人、画家、电影人共同构筑东村的波希米亚场景。作者引用 John Lurie 自传段落，呈现其从明尼苏达迁居纽约、在街头偶得萨克斯后近乎苦行僧式自我训练的经历，揭示 Lounge Lizards 形成的文化土壤。文末戛然而止，未及具体音乐分析，但已为这张现场合辑勾勒出爵士与先锋艺术交织的创作背景，听者可循此脉络理解其冷峻克制、介于自由即兴与后朋克之间的独特声响取向。

items.body: Label: Sunnyside Records, 2026 Personnel - Jason Rigby: tenor and soprano saxophones; Lisa Parrott: alto, soprano, and baritone saxophones; Russ Johnson: trumpet; Cameron Brown: bass; Tony Jefferson: drums. Bassist and composer Cameron Brown has always felt comfortable in both traditional and avant-garde settings, and was an important element in the rhythm sections behind Archie Shepp, Don Pullen, George Adams, George Russell, Dewey Redman, and Don Cherry. Here, he leads a chordless quintet, paying tribute to Cherry as well as his mentor Dannie Richmond, best known for his extensive work with the one-and-only bassist, composer, and bandleader Charles Mingus. This ensemble started as a quartet featuring saxophonist Jason Rigby, trumpeter Russ Johnson, and drummer Tony Jefferson. Saxophonist Lisa Parrott joins them here for a dense, unfiltered session recorded live in concert in 2011. Raw and dense, it often sounds like a jam. The uptempo “ Sheila, It’s You! ”—written for the late jazz vocalist Sheila Jordan—has the three-horn frontline blowing with hard-bop intensity over the hard-charging swing provided by the rhythm section. They alternate solos before intersecting their searing lines with purpose. Conversely, “ Lullaby For George, Don, and Donnie ” is a 3/4 ballad gently propelled by brushes. “ Baby Suite ” is a through-composed response to Cherry’s “cocktail suite” concept. Brown’s three-minute bass monologue—featuring double-stops and thoughtful melodic development—right after the contrapuntal theme leads into faster bass circularity, with Jefferson free to embellish while the horns float above. A spontaneous avant-garde freedom reminiscent of Mingus’ excursions can be felt in the coda that precedes the theme. “ Cocktail Suite ”, which clocks in at 21 minutes and includes Cherry’s “ Remembrance ” and “ OC/DC ”, Jobim’s “ Portrait in Black and White ”, and Redman’s “ Mushi Mushi ”, features some awkward passages and elongated solos with the horns left to roam freely. Incessant walking lines populate the recording, creating an inescapable sense of anticipation. Brown’s “ Rylie’s Bounce ” blooms with a bass solo at the outset and explosive drumming by Jefferson, who throws in some barbed percussive sounds on Richmond’s “ Soft Seas ”, an amusing calypso dance served with humor and panache. Parrott causes some frisson on baritone, while Rigby explores the opposite end of the spectrum on soprano. This piece is put together much more effectively, with a keen sense of time and a divergence from conventional swing. With the interplay controlled at all times and the recording sounding like a classic, Remembrance sometimes rings a bit meandering, yet never disjointed. Favorite Tracks: 02 - Baby Suite ► 03 - Soft Seas ► 07 - Cocktail Suite

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由低音提琴手Cameron Brown领衔一支无和弦乐器五重奏，向Don Cherry、Dannie Richmond等前辈致敬。整体录制于2011年的现场演出，呈现出粗粝、即兴驱动的特质：硬波普的激烈齐奏段落与三拍子抒情慢曲交替展开，21分钟的《Cocktail Suite》整合了Cherry、Jobim、Redman的多首作品，融合行走低音线与自由段落。Brown的低音独白段落运用双音与对位旋律发展，呼应Mingus式的自发表演逻辑。Lisa Parrott的上低音与Jason Rigby的高音形成两端频谱拉伸，Tony Jefferson的鼓声在加力比节奏中带有幽默感。整张专辑虽有自由流动的散漫感，但节奏控制始终保持内在凝聚力，是一份兼具传统根基与先锋精神的现场录音。

items.body: Valencia label Industrial Complexx reissues the various-artists compilation “SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends” on double cassette and digital on October 15, 2026. The 18-track set, originally released by Unknown Pleasures Records in 2014, gathers international minimal synth, electro-punk and industrial acts covering the catalogue of Suicide’s Alan Vega and Martin Rev. SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends by Various Artists The reissue accompanies the Spanish-language publication of “Suicide, delincuentes electrónicos,” an essay on the band by musician and writer Pedro Peñas y Robles, originally published in French and English in 2024 and now released in Spanish by Industrial Complexx. The book traces the duo’s genesis and the chaotic sessions behind their 1977 debut album, drawing on testimony from scene figures including Marc Hurtado of Étant Donnés. ‘SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends’ contributors The tribute pairs Vega and Rev’s original catalogue with reinterpretations from Distel, Radical G, The Horrorist, David Carretta and Jürgen Engler of Die Krupps, Növö, Adan+Ilse featuring Gabi Delgado of D.A.F., Marc Hurtado performing with Alan Vega himself, Liebknecht featuring Kristoffer Grip of Agent Side Grinder, Unknown Celebrities, Laag, Position Parallele, Cruise [ctrl] featuring Richard 23 and Patrick Codenys of Front 242, The Present Moment, Absolute Body Control, Millimetric featuring Dirk Da Davo of The Neon Judgement, Black Egg featuring hausfrau, Simi Nah featuring KGB, and In Death It Ends featuring Usher of Norma Loy. Covered songs include “Che,” “Ghost Rider,” “Cheree,” “Frankie Teardrop,” “Dream Baby Dream” and “Diamonds, Fur Coat, Champagne.” Industrial Complexx describes the collection as channeling “the same abrasive, alienating and futuristic energy” that shaped Suicide’s catalogue. About Suicide Suicide was an American duo formed in New York City in 1970 by vocalist Alan Vega and instrumentalist Martin Rev, initially a trio with guitarist Paul Liebgott before continuing as a two-piece. The group paired Vega’s stream-of-conscious, rockabilly-inflected vocals with Rev’s minimal synthesizer and drum-machine backing, and was among the first acts to use the term “punk music” to describe itself, in 1970. Suicide independently released its debut album, “Suicide,” in 1977 on Red Star Records, featuring “Ghost Rider,” “Frankie Teardrop” and “Cheree.” A second album, “Suicide: Alan Vega and Martin Rev,” followed in 1980 on Ze Records, then “A Way of Life” in 1988, “Why Be Blue” in 1992 and the final studio album, “American Supreme,” in 2002. Vega and Rev also worked separately: Vega collaborated with Andrew Eldritch of The Sisters of Mercy as The Sisterhood in 1986, and with Alex Chilton and Ben Vaughn on “Cubist Blues” in 1996, while both released solo albums throughout their careers. Suicide played its final concert at London’s Barbican Centre on July 9, 2015, before Alan Vega died on July 16, 2016, at age 78. “SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends,” first released via Unknown Pleasures Records in 2014, returns via Industrial Complexx on October 15, 2026, alongside the Spanish edition of Pedro Peñas y Robles’s book on the band.

items.body: One half of the Senior Staff was able to get out to a wholly non-ID:UD related gig over the weekend and catch Calgary’s Mares Of Thrace play a very rhythmically tight and cathartic set of doom metal. As we’ve briefly discussed here and there we’re both fans of a decent amount of metal covering a number of sub-genres, but neither of us are experts. Frankly, sometimes its nice to switch off the part of your brain that needs to be developing informed opinions and producing thoughtful analysis at all times and just enjoy some music simply because you dig it. But speaking of thoughtful analysis (?), let’s get you back to the home front with this week’s tracks. Dismantled Godflesh, “Master And Slave” Justin Broadrick announced earlier this year that he’d be winding Godflesh down for a second time some fifteen-odd years after its reactivation, but was planning two full LPs of new material before that time comes. The first such record sees release on Friday, and while the ratio of dub, electronic, and breaks elements which have always flitted about Godflesh releases had perhaps increased over the last few post-reunion albums, it’s hard not to think that Decay will be going right for the jugular Streetcleaner style based on its opening track. Turn it up and revel in the soothing annihilation of that bass tone. Decay by GODFLESH Grendel, “Dominion” It’s somehow been 7 years since the release of Grendel’s last LP Ascending the Abyss. It’s been a tangible absence in Our offices; JD Tucker has spent the last decade and a half redefining his legacy as an electro-industrial stylist and producer, starting with 2012’s genre-defying Timewave: Zero and the superlative Age of the Disposable Body, the latter being legitimately one of the most important political albums of the 2010s in Our Thing. “Dominion” speaks to the band we’ve come to know Grendel to be while showing some intriguing developments, such as JD’s now accomplished melodic vocal style, some very smooth string programming and sleek modern sound design applied to a classic EBM gallop. All that and lyrics that don’t just decry the social media era but examine the panopticon of control they emerge from? Welcome back Grendel, we missed you. Dominion by Grendel Dismantled, “Zero” Speaking of long-awaited returns, holy shit, there’s new Dismantled. Gary Zon’s long-running project has always been a standard bearer for a version of hard and harsh electro-industrial that maintains the genre’s atmospheric and emotional core. The first track from the forthcoming Endless is “Zero”, a cut that features Zon’s distinctive processed and multi-layered vocals, samples, and some fine string programming for good measure. It’s melancholic, but after a more than half a decade wait (the album was originally teased all the way back in 2021), it’s a sound that feels right. Endless by Dismantled Rosetta Stone, “Shadowban” Porl King’s moved Rosetta Stone through a number of preceding modes since reactivating the legendary second wave of goth rock project as a solo joint seven years back. A forthcoming release looks to keep that trend going (the Executing Nostalgia title feels rather on the nose in that regard) – one half of it will be made up of classic goth covers, continuing in the tradition of Unerotica and last year’s Nothing Is Sacred, while the other half is originals. This first taste of the latter feels like a callback to a very different moment in King’s history, though: the claustrophobic and hazy bass fog of this cut’s a dead ringer for the post witch house loops and grooves which made up the bulk of the voluminous In Death It Ends catalog in the 2010s. Shadowban by Rosetta Stone Control Fields, “Black Anomaly” Some solidly chewy bass sits at the centre of the B-side of the debut single from Tbilisi producer Control Fields, but that’s not the only thing which has us flashing back to 90s EBM and dark electro. The combo of icy programming and classic “hacking the Gibson” style sampling on this goes down as smooth as a Jolt cola being slammed during an all night Quake LAN party. Friction Code by Control Fields Emmon, “Relics (Kris Baha remix)” Kris Baha is one of the most reliable producers that emerged from the techno-body moment, with his canny grasp of gnarly sound design and how to assemble peak time bangers making him a go-to remixer for many artists. For evidece of why and the results why not check out Baha’s mix for Emmon’s “Relics”, taking the pensive and punchy original and giving it a slick peak-time makeover that references breakbeat driven 90’s techno, some psytrance, and some seriously warped synthwork. This’ll singe your nosehairs if you aren’t careful, play loud with caution. The post Tracks: September 21st, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.album: Charlie May / Trusted Farms (ASIPV058)
items.body:
After decades contributing to records where a single riff could transform a dancefloor, Charlie May turns that instinct inward on Trusted Farms. 

 For over thirty years, Charlie has occupied a position that seems increasingly rare in electronic music: the musician’s musician, the person behind the machines, the extra pair of hands in the studio, and quite often, the person responsible for the melody you end up carrying around in your head for weeks on end. 

 Alongside Duncan Forbes as Spooky, Charlie helped shape some of the most important electronic music to emerge from the UK in the early ’90s. That partnership would also sow the seeds for one of Sasha’s defining records: the central riff behind Xpander began life in Spooky’s live material, before Charlie brought the idea into the studio with Sasha and helped transform it into one of electronic music’s most enduring anthems.

 astrangelyisolatedplace · ASIPV058 Charlie May / Trusted Farms [PREVIEWS] 

 Listen closely to Charlie’s work and there’s a particular instinct that keeps returning: knowing when a simple synth line is enough. Knowing which note needs to change. Knowing when repetition stops being repetition and starts becoming the entire reason a track works. More recently, as one-third of Quiet Places on ASIP, he’s taken those same instincts somewhere looser — beatless, gridless and led by improvisation.

 Trusted Farms puts those instincts front and centre.

 Tiny melodic phrases appear and refuse to leave. Synth lines repeat just long enough to become lodged in your head. Parts rub against each other without being tidied into submission. There’s a sharpness and directness to it all amongst the purposeful analogue warmth.

 Some of these tracks feel almost ridiculously simple at first. But simplicity is difficult when you’ve spent decades learning every possible way to complicate something. Many of the parts on Trusted Farms were performed live with minimal editing. A synth line might be doubled, distorted, re-recorded and pushed back through another piece of equipment, but it remains the same idea. Instead of filling the gaps, Charlie works on the weight and character of what is already there. The melodies become physical; slightly worn around the edges.

 For someone whose fingerprints can be found across some genuinely monumental moments in electronic music, Charlie has spent decades knowing what to add. Trusted Farms is about knowing exactly what to leave alone.

 Available on black 12” and digital, mastered by Andreas Lupo LOOP-O Lubich and featuring artwork by Peter Skwiot Smith, Trusted Farms will be available on October 16th 2026.

items._cn_summary: Charlie May 在《Trusted Farms》中将三十余年电子音乐制作经验聚焦于极简合成器旋律的反复雕琢。专辑延续了他在 Quiet Places 中展现的无节拍、脱离网格的即兴倾向，强调以模拟合成器的温暖音色承载短小却执拗的旋律片段。许多段落以现场演奏为主，仅经加倍、失真与重录处理，乐句在重复中逐渐获得重量与磨损感。这张作品不追求复杂度，而以克制与留白为核心——知道哪些音符需要改变、何时停止叠加，让简单的动机成为整首曲目的全部依据。

items.body: Everybody Else’s Life, Too is the latest from Josh Berman, a stalwart of the Chicago scene still somewhat underappreciated outside of his hometown. He has played the gamut of Chicago improvisors (including Mars Williams’ A Very Ayler Xmas project, the all-too-short-lived Michael Zerrang and the Blue Lights, and Ken Vandermark’s Audio One), sneaked across the Atlantic to record with Paul Lytton, Edward Perraud, and Jon Rune Strøm, and led several of his own bands. On this one, he is joined by bassist Jason Roebke – a reliably punchy oft-times sideman of Chicago circles - and the indefatigable drummer Chris Corsano for a live date at Chicago’s Constellation from 2025. I cannot say there is much surprising here if you are familiar with Berman’s previous headline albums. That said, this is more of what this listener wants rather than simply more of the same. Berman clearly has a thing for bop, in its various forms, and maybe the title is even a nod to his appreciation of those who came before and inspired him. The songs on here start with a catchy head, or a few more plodding, smokey ones, and from there break down into spurs, knotty angles, and spindly striations. One could play this album for someone who thought Miles went too far when he went electric, or Coltrane with Ascension, and they would happily bob their head along with Roebke’s walking bass or Corsano’s steady patter behind Berman’s jumpy melodies. But restricting this to such a palatable bridge would miss the other point, which lies in the free form sections that, yes, are tied to the head but in a sensual way that deviates from its rhythm, tune, and key in favor of capturing, extending, and straining the intricacies of a spontaneous moment. Those sections are when Berman stretches into flutters, crackles, and bites, when Roebke leans into timbre, and Corsano eschews rhythm for sound. Those sections are limited; in this case I think for the better. That is not because trio cannot stretch out into the unknown. (Take the eighth cut, Scale, as an example of their exploratory chops.) Instead, it is because they do so within Berman’s bookending melodic confines that set the direction and mark the terminal point. And were those themes not inspired, this would fall flat. But they are and do not. For doubters, just listen to the wonderfully lonesome and wistful closer, Second Look, where Corsano’s brushes lay a soft-rain backdrop to Berman’s and Roebke’s melancholic dialog. Everybody Else’s Life, Too is much in the vein of a different Josh Berman Trio’s A Dance and a Hop (2015) and should be considered an expansion of that project. Again, you might well know what to expect if you have been following Berman already, but that does not make what you hear any less satisfying. Everybody Else’s Life, Too is available download from Bandcamp and a CD from a few choice independent music outlets. See the CvD website for more . Everybody Else's Life, Too by Josh Berman Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._genre: free jazz / improvisation / bop
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由芝加哥资深爵士演奏家Josh Berman领衔的 trio 录制，2025年于芝加哥Constellation现场录音，贝斯手Jason Roebke与鼓手Chris Corsano加盟。Berman在此延续其一贯路线：以bop旋律骨架为出发点，歌曲以抓耳的主题或缓慢烟雾感的乐段开启，随后解构为棱角分明的即兴段落与细碎音层。自由段落中Berman的号声延展为颤动、碎裂与咬合的质感，Roebke转向音色探索，Corsano则以声响取代节律。这些即兴被框定在旋律主题之内，形成方向与终点的对照。专辑与2015年作品《A Dance and a Hop》一脉相承，是该项目的延伸。对于熟悉Berman的听众而言并无太多惊喜，但旋律主题的扎实使整体听感依然满足。

items.album: Floating
items.excerpt: Label: ACT, 2026 Personnel - Emile Parisien: soprano saxophone; Yaron Herman: piano; Linda May Han Oh: bass; Prabhu Edouard: tabla, percussion, voice. French soprano saxophonist and composer Emile Parisien is an eclectic jazz practitioner with inestimable musical gifts that allow him to explore a whole universe of sound. Parisien brings a glowing selection of tunes composed by himself, pianist and longtime collaborator Yaron Herman, and proficient bassist Linda May Han Oh, alongside two covers.
items.body: Label: ACT, 2026 Personnel - Emile Parisien: soprano saxophone; Yaron Herman: piano; Linda May Han Oh: bass; Prabhu Edouard: tabla, percussion, voice. French soprano saxophonist and composer Emile Parisien is an eclectic jazz practitioner with inestimable musical gifts that allow him to explore a whole universe of sound. Parisien brings a glowing selection of tunes composed by himself, pianist and longtime collaborator Yaron Herman, and proficient bassist Linda May Han Oh, alongside two covers. Rounding out the quartet is tabla player and vocalist Prabhu Edouard, who helps establish an organically integrated framework for the leader’s world-fusion aesthetics. This group was formed after a memorable first performance in Paris. Floating opens with Georges Ivanovitch Gurdjieff and Thomas de Hartmann’s “ Asian Songs & Rhythms, No. 40 ”, a peaceful, spiritual tune that, combining Eastern modal traditions with Western classical sensibilities, slowly unfolds with a ternary feel. Parisien employs his intervallic expertise in vibrant phrasing, while Herman evokes distant, serene landscapes. The other cover on the album is Anouar Brahem’s “ Badhra ”—the fantastic opening track of his trio album Thimar—which scintillates with sophistication and enchantment. In the latter, Herman’s clarity of speech and objectivity pair well with the in-and-out lyricism of Parisien, while the duo’s co-written piece, “ Portal ”, keeps the rhythmic momentum going after a dynamic introduction centered on Edouard, who doubles on tabla and voice. Herman’ piano solo on this one is pure delight. On the other hand, Parisien’s “ Bonbon ” is filled with excitement and aligned with Middle Eastern traditions. Herman contributes five compositions of his own: the waltzing ballads “ Olive Branch ” and “ Ruth ”, with the latter acquiring a jazzier, Keith Jarrett-esque vibe before morphing into a more percussive passage over which Parisien’s soprano glides effortlessly; the playful and bluesy “ Nusrat ”; and the stop-and-go flow of “ El Toro ”, a showcase for Oh’s rhythmic adroitness. Sandwiched between the latter two tracks is the bassist’s “ As It Comes And As It Goes ”, a moment of reflection and an opportunity to hear her unaccompanied. According to the bandleader, this is music about peace, poetry, and love, and listeners should be able to feel its emotional appeal as well as the group’s ability to communicate through whatever musical language they choose to mix in. This forward-looking diversity is key, and Parisien’s fusion is not without an airily contemporary touch. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Asian Songs & Rhythms, No 40 ► 04 - Badhra ► 08 - Nusrat
items._genre: world fusion / contemporary jazz / chamber jazz / global fusion
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由法国次中音萨克斯手Emile Parisien领衔，融合东方调式与西方古典语汇，构成一种有机整合的世界融合美学。曲目编排跨越Gurdjieff与de Hartmann的灵性东方旋律、Anouar Brahem的中东情调，以及Herman带有Keith Jarrett气质的爵士叙事。Tabla与低音提琴的节奏层在不同文化语境间自由切换，钢琴的清晰叙事与萨克斯的抒情线条形成对话，体现出和平、诗意与爱的主题概念。整体编曲在跨文化融合方面展现出成熟的工艺水准，但评论中对实验性与即兴深度的描述相对有限，更多聚焦在氛围与情绪层面。

items.body:
There is a substantial list of attributes that sets Ran Blake apart from every other innovative pianist of the past sixty-plus years, each of which falls under one of two headings: his choice of materials and his treatments of them. The former is based on Blake’s ability to hear connections between materials for which “disparate” is an inadequate descriptor. Who else would sequence Max Roach’s “Mendacity” and “Saving All My Love for You” – or “On Top of Old Smokey” and Michel Legrand’s “Watch What Happens”? Nobody, because what Blake does is unique. He doesn’t interpret materials as much as administer an MRI, revealing the connective tissues and vital organs as vividly, if not more so, than the skeletal structure. In the process, Blake makes the familiar sound radically new.

Blake’s collaborations with singers are central to his work. The current critical consensus is that his groundbreaking work with Jeanne Lee overshadows everything since, the respective qualities of notables like Christine Correa and Sara Serpa notwithstanding. Roots & Byways circumvents the edifice The Newest Sound Around has become, primarily because Dominique Eade takes a different tact. She is not as rooted as Correa – or Lee, for that matter – in Billie Holiday, and she is not as committed to understatement as Serpa. Like both Correa and Serpa, Eade can shape a song syllable by syllable and render a highly personal interpretation. It is Eade’s palpably deep joy in singing that sets her apart, one that is not only bursting at the seams on showstoppers like the Whitney Houston megahit, but one that even seeps into noirish songs like Mingus’ “Portrait.” It is the key to her relatability and appeal, and to that of the album, as well.
items.label: Sunnyside SCS 1813
items._genre: avant-garde jazz / vocal improvisation / experimental piano
items._cn_summary: 兰·布莱克与歌手多米尼克·伊德的合作专辑《Roots & Byways》展现了极具个人特色的艺术方法。布莱克的钢琴演奏以独特的选曲逻辑著称，将风格迥异的曲目并置——从马克斯·罗奇的《Mendacity》到《Saving All My Love for You》，从《On Top of Old Smokey》到勒格朗的《Watch What Happens》——揭示旋律与和声之间隐蔽的连接结构。评论将布莱克的手法比作对作品的"核磁共振扫描"，而非传统意义上的诠释。专辑也涉及布莱克与歌手长期合作传统的讨论，将伊德与此前合作的珍妮·李、克里斯汀·科雷亚、萨拉·塞尔帕进行对照。伊德的演唱特点在于逐音节雕琢歌曲形态的能力，以及在不同情绪歌曲中流露的真实愉悦感，这成为专辑感染力的核心来源。整体而言，这是一张在选材与处理手法上都极具实验性的爵士人声专辑。

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由小提琴家Ján Kružliak Jr.主导，延续其先前OĽUN项目路线，将斯洛伐克传统民间音乐与古典音乐传统进行深度对接。三个组合参与演奏：Spectrum弦乐四重奏、传统风格的Nogaband弦乐四人组，以及女声演唱团体Ulijanky。曲目主要改编自斯洛伐克作曲家Eugen Suchon、Ilja Zeljenka、Alexander Moyzes以及深入斯洛伐克采集民间音乐的匈牙利作曲家Béla Bartók的作品，每首曲目的民间音乐源头（演奏者和村落地点）均在唱片说明中标注。这些改编与演奏并未采用管弦乐式的圆润处理，而是保留了民间音乐的能量与声乐传统音色，展现出演奏者与歌手对这一传统的深入理解和浸润。评论强调这是一部扎实而丰富的作品，演奏与演唱兼具技巧与精神力量。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. More to hear: United States of Alchemy - Songs of Compassion (Review) Dani Jan� - Vida (Review)

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items.body: Review by Abrasmatheus — Wish You Were Here is one of those albums that does not need to be excessively complex to feel progressive. Released in 1975, it combines progressive rock, psychedelic rock, art rock and space rock into an incredibly cohesive and atmospheric experience. I would not consider it one of Pink Floyd's most overtly progressive albums, but its careful compositions, long instrumental developments, experimental production and thematic coherence make it a very strong progressive rock work.The atmosphere is probably the album's greatest strength. It is contemplative, melancholic, emotional and, at times, almost intellectual in the way its themes are presented. The production has aged remarkably well, with every instrument occupying its own space in the mix. The synthesizers and keyboards of Richard Wright are particularly impressive, adding an essential dimension to the album's sound.The centerpiece is undoubtedly "Shine On You Crazy Diamond", which I consider a masterpiece in its own right. I prefer to experience its different sections as one complete work rather than treating them as separate pieces. The song contains excellent instrumental development, especially in the guitars, drums and synthesizers. David Gilmour's guitar work is outstanding, combining technical ability with an enormous amount of emotional expression. Wright's keyboards are equally important, creating much of the psychedelic and spacious atmosphere that defines the piece.The emotional weight of "Shine On You Crazy Diamond" is also increased by its connection to Syd Barrett, whose work with Pink Floyd I greatly admire. Knowing that the song was written as a tribute to him gives the piece an additional emotional dimension. The feeling of loss and nostalgia is deeply present without overwhelming the music itself."Welcome to the Machine" is another major highlight. Its synthesizer work is simply magnificent, and the electronic textures create an almost mechanical atmosphere that perfectly complements the song's subject matter. The composition is less progressive in a traditional structural sense, but its sound design and atmosphere are remarkably creative. I would give the synthesizers an almost absurd 10/10 ? or, jokingly, 1,000,000/10. This is one of the clearest examples of how Pink Floyd could use studio production itself as part of the composition.The lyrics also contribute considerably to the album's thematic unity. Alongside the tribute to Syd Barrett, the record deals with the music industry and the way it can become destructive and dehumanizing. "Welcome to the Machine" and "Have a Cigar" are particularly effective in this regard. Even though these themes were written in the 1970s, they remain strikingly relevant today."Have a Cigar" is another very enjoyable track. Roy Harper's vocals work surprisingly well and have some similarities to Roger Waters' voice. The song is more accessible than some of the album's other material, but it still fits naturally into the overall concept.The title track, "Wish You Were Here", is probably the most commercially accessible song on the album. I personally rate it slightly below the other tracks, at 7/10, but it still serves an important role in the album as a whole. Its lyrics and emotional character provide another perspective on the themes of absence, loss and alienation.One of the things I appreciate most about Wish You Were Here is how naturally the tracks connect to each other. The album can almost feel like one long composition, rather than simply a collection of individual songs. The transitions, recurring atmosphere and production choices create an unusually strong sense of unity.From a progressive perspective, I would describe the album as moderately progressive. It is not constantly concerned with complex time signatures, virtuosity or extremely elaborate structures. Instead, its progressive qualities come from the development of ideas, extended instrumental passages, experimentation with sound, thematic coherence and the willingness to let atmosphere become a fundamental part of the composition.The instrumentation is excellent throughout. Gilmour's guitars are a major highlight, Wright's keyboards and synthesizers are perhaps the most distinctive element of the album for me, Nick Mason's drumming contributes effectively to the long developments, and the saxophone adds another color to the sound. The engineering and production are also outstanding, particularly in the way the instruments and effects are separated and integrated into the overall soundscape.The album's strongest qualities are "Shine On You Crazy Diamond," Richard Wright's synthesizers and keyboards, and David Gilmour's guitars and vocals. I honestly don't have any significant weaknesses to point out. Even though "Wish You Were Here" itself is the most commercial track and the one I personally rate lowest, it is still an important part of the complete experience.Overall, Wish You Were Here is an album in which you can become completely absorbed in the atmosphere of the music. It is contemplative, melancholic, psychedelic and emotionally powerful, while remaining carefully composed and remarkably cohesive.Alongside Meddle and Atom Heart Mother, it is among my favorite Pink Floyd albums.Essential for anyone interested in atmospheric and psychedelic progressive rock.
items._genre: progressive rock / psychedelic rock / art rock / space rock
items._cn_summary: Pink Floyd 1975年专辑以渐进摇滚为骨架，融合迷幻、太空摇滚与艺术摇滚的质感，形成极具氛围感的整体体验。评论着重指出专辑的氛围营造是最突出之处：Richard Wright的合成器与键盘铺陈出冥想、忧郁而情感充沛的声场，制作精良，各乐器在混音中各得其所。核心曲目《Shine On You Crazy Diamond》作为向Syd Barrett致敬之作，以器乐发展为线索，将Gilmour的吉他、键盘与鼓组编织为统一的整体，情感厚度来自于对失去与怀旧的隐喻而非直白宣泄。《Welcome to the Machine》以合成器纹理构建机械感氛围，展示了Pink Floyd将录音室制作本身纳入作曲的手法。歌词层面，专辑触及音乐工业的异化主题，在当下语境中仍具现实意义。整体而言，评论视此作为氛围驱动、主题统一的渐进摇滚佳作，虽非Pink Floyd最具前卫野心之作，却在情绪深度与制作层面展现出成熟。

items.body: Zwickau’s Elektrisch Festival returns on 24 October 2026 with a line-up that makes a convincing argument for electronic music as a continuum rather than a museum of separate generations. At one end stands Portion Control, active since 1979 and fundamental to the development of British industrial electronics; around them are Hungarian EBM veterans Escalator, the much newer KRIEG-B, and the contemporary projects OSZYLAYTER and Cyborg Projekt X. The 19th Elektrisch Festival takes place at Club Seilerstraße, Seilerstraße 1B, 08056 Zwickau. Doors open at 19:00, with the programme beginning at 20:00. The final line-up announced by organiser emmobiz Records is Portion Control, Escalator, OSZYLAYTER, Cyborg Projekt X and KRIEG-B. A festival with a rather unusual history Elektrisch is not a newly invented festival carrying an impressive number. Its history reaches back well before the current revival. Contemporary reports document the 11th edition in 2007, the 12th in 2008, the 13th in 2009, and two editions, numbers 14 and 15, in 2010, then held at Zwickau’s BPM Club. Artists appearing during that period included names such as Absolute Body Control, Birmingham 6, Tyske Ludder and The Klinik. Then Elektrisch disappeared for fourteen years. emmobiz Records revived it in 2024 with the 16th Elektrisch Festival, now at Club Seilerstraße. That return was already sold out months in advance and brought together Calva Y Nada, Cat Rapes Dog, Digital Factor and Accessory. The 17th edition followed in October 2025 with Test Dept, NZ, In Strict Confidence, Supreme Court and To Avoid. In February 2026, the 18th Elektrisch expanded across two evenings, separating a synthpop-oriented first night from a harder EBM/electro programme on the second. That history makes the 2026 autumn line-up apt: Elektrisch has repeatedly connected artists from different phases of underground electronic music instead of reducing EBM to one historical period. Portion Control The obvious historical heavyweight is Portion Control. Formed in London in 1979, the group emerged from the early British industrial-electronic underground and became important for its use of synthesisers, drum machines and sampling long before those methods became standard practice. Their influence has subsequently been acknowledged in connection with artists including Skinny Puppy, Front Line Assembly, Nine Inch Nails, Orbital and Nitzer Ebb; they also toured with Depeche Mode in 1984. But calling Portion Control a heritage act would miss what remains interesting about them. They returned in the 2000s and have continued producing new work rather than maintaining the early catalogue. This August they released “1983-86 – Hit The Pulse to Purge…”, their first major Artoffact archival box, while their official site simultaneously continues to define the project rather succinctly as “uncompromising dark electronic audio.” Zwickau is currently one of only two forthcoming live appearances listed on their Bandcamp. Escalator Escalator brings another kind of history to the evening. The Hungarian project was founded in Budapest in 1988 by 2RT+TB and belongs to the late-’80s/early-’90s generation of European Electronic Body Music. Its musical roots lie in the harder intersection of EBM and industrial electronics, with early influences including Kraftwerk, Throbbing Gristle, Cabaret Voltaire, Clock DVA and Front 242. Escalator’s history has been anything but linear; long gaps between releases and activity have been part of the project, yet its work has remained closely associated with the physical, stripped-back mechanics of classic body music. Their presence next to Portion Control is more than an “old-school” pairing: the two acts come from different geographical and chronological points in the development of electronic body music. OSZYLAYTER The German OSZYLAYTER represents a much more recent strand of the line-up. Public biographical information on the project is relatively sparse, so it is better not to manufacture a grand history that isn’t there. What can be verified is a growing Bandcamp catalogue including “Hate This Day”, “Lover Boy”, “Free Girls” and “Dig It in the Dirt”, while current Elektrisch coverage places the project on the modern dark-electro/industrial side of the bill. In the context of Elektrisch, that relative newness is actually useful. This isn’t five bands demonstrating variations of exactly the same established EBM formula; OSZYLAYTER helps shift the evening toward newer club electronics and shows where some of those older physical principles have travelled. Cyborg Projekt X Cyborg Projekt X is similarly one of the less extensively documented names on the programme. The confirmed festival announcement places the project alongside OSZYLAYTER as part of the contemporary dark-electro and industrial side of the line-up, with an emphasis on forceful, club-oriented electronics. That makes Cyborg Projekt X something of the unknown variable of the evening, especially for listeners arriving primarily for the established EBM names. In a festival whose history has always mixed recognised acts with smaller projects, that is hardly out of character. KRIEG-B KRIEG-B is much newer as a project but comes with considerable history behind its members. The duo was formed in June 2023 by Dominique Lallement, known from Kriegbereit, Cobalt 60 and K-Bereit, and Benoît Buyse, associated with Dreadfool, Anamorphosis and Nihiliste. The project describes its music as a meeting point between industrial electronics, EBM and darkwave, drawing on several decades of electronic music rather than one specific period. Their debut album “War Drums’ Resonance” arrived in November 2024, with tracks including “S.C.S.N”, “Parabellum”, “Artificial Minds”, “Truth Lies” and “King of Emptiness”. In a sense, KRIEG-B makes a neat closing piece to the Elektrisch concept: a young project constructed by musicians carrying several earlier generations of European industrial electronics with them. More than the line-up The revived Elektrisch has also developed a strong physical-release component. The 18th edition was accompanied by exclusive 10-inch festival vinyl releases, while emmobiz has already announced a V.A. “19. Elektrisch Festival” 10-inch connected to this year’s event. The appeal of the 19th edition goes beyond Portion Control finally returning to Zwickau. The five acts represent very different positions within the same broad history: British industrial experimentation, Hungarian old-school EBM, contemporary German dark electronics, and a new Franco-Belgian project carrying the experience of earlier industrial formations into something current. That is probably the strongest reason to pay attention to Elektrisch. After a fourteen-year absence, the festival did not return simply to recreate the period in which it originally existed. Its current identity depends on putting that history into the same room with what came after it. 19. Elektrisch Festival: date, venue and line-up Elektrisch Festival 24 October 2026 Club Seilerstraße Seilerstraße 1B, 08056 Zwickau, Germany Line-up: Portion Control Escalator OSZYLAYTER Cyborg Projekt X KRIEG-B Doors: 19:00 Start: 20:00 Tickets are available through emmobiz Records.

items._cn_summary: 这是一篇关于德国茨维考第19届Elektrisch音乐节的报道，而非传统意义上的专辑乐评。文章梳理了该音乐节从2007年至今的历史脉络，呈现其如何跨越不同世代串联英国工业电子元老与新晋地下艺人。核心重点在于1980年代工业电子先驱Portion Control的历史地位及其对Skinny Puppy、Nine Inch Nails等后辈的影响，同时呈现了Escalator、KRIEG-B等匈牙利及当代工业/EBM厂牌的阵容。内容主要提供演出时间、地点、阵容等资讯信息，并简要追溯了音乐节的传承脉络，缺少对声音设计、具体作品或艺术手法的深入分析。整体偏向新闻性报道，对于关注暗潮与工业电子场景的听众具有参考价值。

items.body: Ms Xxan released the nine-track album “Make Yourself the Lie” on September 8, 2026, via VuMantra Records, available as a free, name-your-price download on Bandcamp. Ms Xxan performs the album’s spoken word poetry herself, processing her voice through synthesized effects and building the backing from dark ambient and noise-industrial soundscapes, with every credit on the record, from writing through final mix, going to her alone. The album carries a content warning for strong and explicit lyrics; depression under present-day conditions runs through its themes, and the nine tracks grow steadily heavier as the sequence progresses: “make yourself the lie.”, “psychic break.”, “doctrine of harm.”, “dissociative parallels.”, “crossing over.”, “discontinuance.”, “disremember.”, “anhedonia.” and “hatchling.” The same material is also published in episode form as the “Ms Xxan” podcast, available on Apple Podcasts and Audiomack, and streams on SoundCloud alongside the Bandcamp release. Make Yourself the Lie by Ms Xxan About Ms Xxan Ms Xxan writes and produces spoken word and industrial noise music from her current base in the Pacific Northwest, a home she plans to leave before long. “Make Yourself the Lie”, released September 8, 2026, is her album for VuMantra Records, a Berlin-based label founded by Vū (Vince Gagliardi) in 2019, who also records as The Nent and LAGÁN. VuMantra describes its output as “endarkening rhythms for dystopic sub-cultures”, with a catalog built on percussive, ritualistic and tribalistic electronic music. “Make Yourself the Lie” was written, performed, composed, produced and mixed entirely by Ms Xxan, and stands as her first release documented on the label alongside the parallel “Ms Xxan” podcast series carrying the same material.

items.body: Italian musician Ystrith released the seven-track dark ambient debut album “The M Rites” on 2 September 2026, self-issued on Bandcamp and also available on Spotify. Across its seven tracks, Ystrith works with Mithraic mystery-cult imagery, the Roman-era worship of the god Mithras, pulling on details like its buried temples and the weathered carvings its followers left behind. The M Rites by Ystrith Ystrith described the album to Side-Line as concerned not only with the surviving relics of the Mithraic cult, but with “the unbridgeable distance between the surviving objects of the cult and the experiences that have been lost with time.” The seven tracks – “Cautes”, “Fading Gates (of Cosmic Enlightenment)”, “Marble Tauroctonies”, “Myth of the Petrogenesis”, “Voces Magicae”, “Solstice at the Spelaeum” and “Cautopates” – take their titles directly from Mithraic iconography and ritual: Cautes and Cautopates are the torch-bearing twin attendants of Mithras in Roman relief carvings, while “tauroctonies” refers to the bull-slaying scene at the centre of Mithraic imagery. Ystrith has described the record’s musical language as moving through “slow metamorphoses, obsessive repetition and dark, suspended atmospheres,” sustained across the album’s running time to match its ritual subject matter. About Ystrith Ystrith is an Italian musician who records ambient and dark ambient music. “The M Rites”, released 2 September 2026, is the project’s debut album, presented as a sustained meditation on the Mithraic mysteries rather than a single-themed track or EP. The release is available to stream on Bandcamp and Spotify.
items._genre: dark ambient / ritual ambient / drone
items._cn_summary: 意大利音乐人Ystrith首张专辑《The M Rites》以密特拉教神秘仪式为概念核心，七首曲目直接取材于罗马时期密特拉神的图像志与崇拜遗迹，如双火炬侍从Cautes与Cautopates、屠牛图景tauroctonies、洞穴神龛spelaeum等。音乐语言强调缓慢的形态演变、执念般的重复律动与幽暗悬停的氛围，试图在残存的物质遗存与已流逝的崇拜经验之间建立聆听通道。整张专辑被构建为一场持续的冥想，而非松散的曲目集合，由音乐人在Bandcamp与Spotify自助发行。编曲手法贴合仪式主题，以暗潮氛围的悬浮质感承载考古意象，但在声音设计层面并未展示出突破类型的实验性，整体呈现为概念明确、语境统一的暗潮氛围作品。
