items.body: More than twenty years after Agonoize emerged from Berlin, there is very little ambiguity left about what the name represents. The band built its identity around severe electronic rhythm, distorted vocals, confrontation and a live language that made physical excess part of the music rather than decoration around it. Their own terminology, Hellektro, became closely associated with the harder end of dark electro and aggrotech, combining EBM, industrial and dark-electronic structures with an unusually direct lyrical vocabulary. Agonoize themselves have never seemed especially interested in respecting the borders of those labels. That history also explains why a short conversation with Chris L in 2026 becomes more interesting than a routine tour update. The existing catalogue carries considerable weight, the visual mythology of the band is instantly recognisable, and songs written years ago remain embedded in club culture. But Chris is not speaking about preservation. After a serious illness interrupted both his physical momentum and his songwriting, he is working on new Agonoize material again, while approaching the band with a strikingly uncomplicated principle: he still makes music because he wants to. Ahead of Agonoize’s 25 September appearance at Klub Łącznik in Wrocław, where they play alongside System Noire and Antibody, I caught up with Chris L about returning to songwriting, refusing genre boxes, anger as creative material, performing after illness and why getting older has done very little to make Agonoize more polite. The Wrocław event features full sets from Agonoize and System Noire, with Antibody as special guest and an Angst Factor aftershow with DJane Nox Occultae and DJ Bjørn. Chris L on Agonoize in 2026 Karo: Agonoize have existed for more than two decades now. What does the band need to mean to you personally in 2026 for it still to be worth continuing? Chris: Why shouldn’t it be worth it? I make music because I love it. That’s really the most important reason. As long as I still have something to say and the passion to do it, it will always be worth continuing. Karo: “Revelation Six Six Sick” is already five years old. Are you actively working towards a new Agonoize chapter, and if so, what has changed in the way you want the band to sound? Chris: Five years ago, I was knocked off my feet by a serious illness. It took a long time to find the strength and inspiration to write new songs again. Now I’m working on new material. Time will tell… Karo: “Adios, Goodbye!” with Antibody was one of the more recent glimpses of your writing outside the existing Agonoize catalogue, and now you are sharing the stage in Poland. Did that collaboration open any ideas you would actually like to take further? Chris: “Adios, Goodbye” is not a musical composition by Agonoize. It’s simply a lyric I wrote. The finished song then sat unused for more than a year, for whatever reason. Jan from Antibody is a permanent part of Agonoize, but this song has nothing to do with the Agonoize album that is currently in the works. Karo: Aggrotech has gone through periods of enormous visibility and others when people almost seemed embarrassed by the term. Do you still identify strongly with that scene, or has Agonoize outgrown the usefulness of the label? Chris: I’ve never tried to put a specific musical label on Agonoize. Agonoize is Agonoize. We make our music the way it feels right to us, and I’ve never been interested in putting the band into a box. Karo: I first saw you at WGT many years ago, when there was literally a warning that “there will be blood on the dancefloor.” Back then, the provocation felt genuinely confrontational. Has your own relationship with shock and theatrical violence changed as both you and the audience have grown older? Chris: Agonoize has always been known for addressing subjects that other people don’t dare to talk about. I’m loud, I’m uncomfortable, and I think that’s a good thing. Being different has always been important to me. I don’t have to please everyone. I am who I am. And that has nothing to do with age either. Our fans range from 8 to 70 years old. Music doesn’t have an age limit. Karo: A show with such a recognisable visual language can eventually become something audiences expect rather than something that unsettles them. How do you stop an Agonoize concert from turning into a ritual recreation of its own mythology? Chris: The lyrics I write speak a very clear language and create a very clear picture. I don’t want to hide things behind unnecessary metaphors or sugarcoat them. If I have something to say, I say it directly. Karo: Your lyrics have always used anger very directly. What genuinely makes Chris L angry enough to write about in 2026, and has that anger become more focused with age, or less? Chris: Just look at the world around you. Everything that is happening out there becomes part of the stories we write. We live in a terrible world, and in many ways it seems to be getting worse rather than better. There is just as much anger, frustration and darkness in the world as there has ever been. Of course, all of that finds its way into my lyrics and, ultimately, into my music. Karo: You played M’era Luna again this summer and will soon move into a much more immediate club setting in Wrocław. Does the scale of the room actually change the way you perform, or is Agonoize supposed to overwhelm the space regardless of its size? Chris: I’ve always preferred playing small clubs. There’s something special about being close to the audience, with no barriers and no distance between us. That direct connection is what I love about live shows. And ultimately, it doesn’t depend on the size of the venue. We perform in front of 10,000 people with the same intensity as we do in front of 150. Karo: Agonoize have a catalogue full of songs audiences expect to hear. When constructing a set now, how do you balance that collective memory against your own need not to spend the evening reproducing the past? Chris: Every show is different. The combination of old and new songs is important, and that mixture should be something people can feel at every show. In the past, two-and-a-half to four-and-a-half-hour shows were not unusual for me. Because of my illness, that’s unfortunately no longer possible. But a shorter show can still be just as intense and uncompromising. Karo: Looking ahead, what do you want the next phase of Agonoize to prove, not to people who already know exactly what “Bis das Blut gefriert” means to them, but to somebody encountering the band for the first time now? Chris: I have nothing to prove to anyone except myself. I just want to be able to do what I’ve always been best at: making music. Ultimately, that’s all I want. About Agonoize Formed in Berlin in 2002, Agonoize became one of the most recognisable names in the harder European electro scene. Their official biography describes the project through a collision of industrial, EBM and dark electro, while the band has long used the term Hellektro for its own particularly abrasive variant of that language. From the early “Paranoid Destruction” period through records and releases such as “Assimilation”, “Blutgruppe Jesus”, “Bis das Blut gefriert” and the later “Revelation Six Six Sick”, aggression has remained central, but so has Chris L’s insistence on direct language and subjects designed to create discomfort rather than polite distance. Side-Line previously spoke with the band in 2020 for the ‘Click Interview’ with Agonoize. The theatrical violence of the concerts, including the band’s notorious “Blutshow”, became part of that identity, but the interview above suggests something more useful about Agonoize in 2026: beneath all the blood, noise and provocation, the continuation of the band still depends on something remarkably basic, Chris L wanting to write music again. Agonoize live, upcoming dates The band’s site marks the Wrocław and Bärenstein dates specifically as Blutshows. 25 September 2026 – Klub Łącznik, Wrocław, Poland (with System Noire and Antibody, doors 19:00, Angst Factor aftershow with DJane Nox Occultae and DJ Bjørn) – Blutshow 24 October 2026 – Dark Dance Treffen, Mannheim, Germany 11 December 2026 – Unholy X-Mas, Bärenstein, Germany – Blutshow 12 December 2026 – Unholy X-Mas, Bärenstein, Germany – Blutshow 25 December 2026 – Dark Storm, Chemnitz, Germany 9 January 2027 – Fabrik, Bruchsal, Germany 6 February 2027 – From Hell, Erfurt, Germany 16-18 April 2027 – Dark Malta, Malta 16 October 2027 – ORWOhaus, Berlin, Germany

items.body: Manufracture Music release the single “System Apathy” on 20 October 2026, under a pre-order campaign already live on Bandcamp. The Vienna-based project, run by producer Valerian Steel, built the track entirely on analog synthesizers, drum machines and raw voltage, with no software instruments involved. System Apathy by Manufracture Music The Bandcamp description describes the release as continuing the project’s A.C.I. concept, short for Analog Core Industrial: “Manufracture Music operates on a strict hardware-first philosophy. […] Forged in Vienna, ‘System Apathy’ is built entirely on unforgiving analog synthesizers, drum machines, and raw voltage. The physical behavior of the machines – their limitations, imperfections, and textures – becomes the composition itself.” Steel described the approach directly to Side-Line as “a cold, relentless EBM transmission born from technological friction and dystopian sound design.” Manufracture Music’s second A.C.I. release “System Apathy” follows “The Scene Lies (A.C.I. Manifesto)“, the two-track statement Manufracture Music released on 14 August 2026 that introduced A.C.I. as a stated concept: hardware-only production positioned against generative AI tools in the electronic underground. Where that release took the form of a spoken-word manifesto, “System Apathy” returns the project to song form while keeping the same zero-software constraint. About Manufracture Music Manufracture Music is the industrial, EBM and darkwave project of producer Valerian Steel, based in Vienna, Austria. He also runs the dance-oriented Fourtyfication*5 and the ambient-leaning Music of Synergia under his own name, and has worked with a vocalist credited only as Enzo across several Manufracture Music tracks. The debut album “Fractured Empires” appeared in early 2025, followed by the “Mormon” EP on 29 March 2025 and a run of singles through 2025 and 2026, including “Isolated”, “Ghosts” featuring Enzo, “Blood Syntax”, “Hateration”, “Tearfall”, “End of Life”, “Null Rite System” featuring Enzo, “Kinetic Decay”, “Skip My Tracks” and “Synthetic Species”. “The Scene Lies (A.C.I. Manifesto)” introduced the A.C.I. concept on 14 August 2026, and “System Apathy” now becomes the second release built under that same hardware-only method, due 20 October 2026.

items._cn_summary: Manufracture Music 即将发行单曲《System Apathy》，延续其 A.C.I.（Analog Core Industrial）概念，全部由模拟合成器、鼓机和原始电压信号构建，不使用任何软件乐器。这是该项目的第二张硬件限定作品，承接2026年8月的宣言式双曲《The Scene Lies》。制作人 Valerian Steel 来自维也纳，将硬件的物理局限、缺陷与质感直接转化为作曲素材，强调反生成式AI工具的立场。歌曲回到歌曲形式而非宣言体裁，试图在零软件约束下完成一首冷酷、持续推进的EBM作品。项目此前已发行首张专辑和多张单曲，横跨工业、暗潮和EBM领域，这次尝试是对纯模拟制作哲学的一次集中表达。

items.body: Ahead of a comprehensive box set of live recordings, Richard Foster considers the 'other' Joy Division that barely gets mentioned; the live powerhouse that motored its way across Britain and Europe Joy Division live by Martin O'Neill As the old line goes, we tell ourselves stories in order to live. Sometimes we do this speculatively, through other people’s lives. This kind of speculation also drives the discourse around Joy Division’s brief and tragic history. The post Update Factory Settings: Joy Division Live appeared first on The Quietus.

items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评聚焦Joy Division官方即将发行的现场录音与影像合集《Eternal (Live)》，作者Richard Foster试图重新审视这支乐队作为现场演出者的身份，而非仅限于其悲剧性的录音室遗产。评论指出合集中包含大量未发行素材，影像部分由多位知名乐队摄影师担纲。文章意图挖掘Joy Division作为现场实力派被忽视的一面，回顾其在英国及欧洲巡演时期的能量与张力。由于正文内容较短且更接近预告性介绍，深入的音乐分析与演奏层面的细节讨论相对有限。整体作为对暗潮、后朋克历史经典乐队的现场档案回顾，对关注该领域的听众具有一定参考价值。

items.body: Review by Mauro_2112 — Yes's only concept album and perhaps their most controversial one, Tales from Topographic Oceans is a very ambitious (some would say pretentious even) record that pretty much embodies all of the excess and extravagance of prog. That characteristic, however, sometimes is for its detriment. Throught its more than 80 minutes, the album can sometimes feel pretty tedious, featuring a lot of material that just doesn't compare to Yes's more widely agreed upon masterpieces, however every song is still generaly pretty good, especialy The Revealing Science of God which at least in my opinion is one Yes's best Epics. items._genre: symphonic prog / progressive rock / art rock
items._cn_summary: Yes乐队1973年发行的《Tales from Topographic Oceans》是乐队唯一的概念专辑，也是前卫摇滚史上颇具争议的作品。整张专辑时长超过80分钟，由四个长篇乐章构成，展现了乐队在巅峰时期对宏大叙事的追求。乐评指出，专辑体现了前卫摇滚的极致与铺张，但部分段落冗长拖沓，与乐队其他被广泛认可的杰作相比，素材的精炼程度有所欠缺。不过，乐评认为每首作品的质量仍属上乘，尤其是《The Revealing Science of God》一曲，被视为Yes最优秀的史诗级作品之一。整体而言，这是一次充满野心的音乐实验，乐评者将其定位为一次愉悦的聆听体验。

items.body: Review by alainPP — Uncompromising art rock for a fresh sound, minimalist and captivating alternative electro-prog."My Blistering Mind" boasts a distinctive sound, phrased vocals, and electronic, synth-heavy orchestration reminiscent of Porcupine Tree. A final mantra-like repetition of the gentle chorus shifts between pop, cold wave, and Bowie-esque dance-pop-rock, all set to poignant lyrics about mental fragility. "The Mandatory Prize" features a synthetic riff on electric piano, a long, melancholic, and pervasive melody set to lyrics by Dick, with a sound reminiscent of Steve Wilson. Malcolm's voice is ever-present, pale, cold, and robotic, mirroring the synth pads in a new prog style. But that riff is truly gut-wrenching. "Never Really Felt Like Home," with its ambient, hypnotic, and contemplative intro, and Kathryn's deep flute, is a symbol of tranquility. The piccolo allows for a drift into a cinematic-melancholic space where the low guitar solo amplifies this beatific, solemn instrumental. "Smile, Smile, Smile," already seen on the EP, has a haunting metronomic sound on the vibrating bass, the keyboard unfolding, flirting with Esth�sie, the addictive vocals leading to saturation. An electronic Wilson, like his side project No-Man. A stressful, redundant finale leading to musical madness through its endless repetition, the lyrics cruelly explaining this moment of schizoid disarray. "Intermission," as its name suggests, is an instrumental on bass and drums with a jazzy piano, a way of dreaming about the evolution of jazz today. The ensuing Mellotron chills the ears before the colorful piano nods to the works of Joe Jackson."Parallel Lives," with its hushed vocals and contemplative ballad-like feel, sees Kathryn's guitar work on the chorus amplify its solemnity. The effective rhythmic foundation drives this lament, reminiscent of Springsteen's "Streets of Philadelphia." The eponymous track plunges into the depths of Wavy's pop. "Eversion," one of the longer pieces, meanders with lyrics reminiscent of Kate Bush, its orchestration blending neoclassical, synth, and electronic elements, inspired by Steve Wilson. A piano and synth interlude precedes the electric return and Malcolm's vocals, sly, dark, and haughty. The guitar solo brightens the ear, and the sound returns with hypnotic, syncopated percussion, amplifying the progressive, schizophrenic feel. "Pretty Blue Fox" opens with a modern, electro-synth feel, reminiscent of Tangerine Dream in the 70s. It's a blend of electro and prog, with a satisfying mid-section, scraping away at the repetitive sounds of Philip Glass for a restrained, immersive, orgasmic finale ? pure bliss. "Just Another Thing" returns to new prog rock with its piercing, guttural vocals; you'll want to try these breathless vocalizations yourself. There's a hint of Bowie, a sound reminiscent of Simple Minds, a dynamic track with a neo-Marillion-esque keyboard solo, recounting Malcolm's retinal mishaps. "Dropping The Mask" is another instrumental with an electrified, upbeat tempo and bouncy keyboard, a nod to Tangerine Dream in the 80s ? groovy, energetic, and catchy. "Just Hold On (Pts 1 & 2)" opens with a religious, elegiac intro, the soaring choir drifting into hyperspace?a fitting way to escape this groundbreaking album. A striking mix of languid atmosphere and archaic feel, thanks to a guitar emerging from a cloud of Olympus, the solo spreading to the heavens. Malcolm finally appears on this melting synth, the drums merely controlling the rhythm. A solemn ambiance is created by the double bass, the deep vocals, the ephemeral piano, and the final, melancholic guitar outro, a meditative and hopeful finale. A truly beautiful and contemplative ending. "My Blistering Mind," in a shorter, perhaps faster version, and "The Mandatory Prize" are released as radio edits, destined for the airwaves of a better world.HATS OFF GENTLEMEN IT'S ADEQUATE blends vocal and purely instrumental tracks, delivering electronic art-rock with contemporary classical touches. A modern progressive rock sound for the new millennium. (4.5)

items._cn_summary: 这是一张以合成器与电子音色为主导的前卫跨界专辑，融合了冷波、流行旋律与艺术摇滚的多重脉络。制作人Malcolm以机械化、苍白的人声配合合成器垫底，营造出与Porcupine Tree和No-Man一脉相承的氛围感。曲目如《My Blistering Mind》在轻柔副歌与冷波节奏间切换，歌词聚焦于精神层面的脆弱；《Never Really Felt Like Home》以长笛与低音吉他构建电影化的沉静空间；《Eversion》则以新古典、电子与合成器交织出片段式、略带分裂感的叙事。Kathryn的吉他和长笛为整体音色增添了沉思与悲悯的层次，间奏段落融入爵士钢琴与Mellotron致敬传统。专辑在情感密度与旋律可听性之间取得平衡，实验性主要体现在声音设计与结构编排上，而非彻底的声音解构，整体偏向Porcupine Tree、Steven Wilson式的新派前卫路线。

items.body: Review by alainPP — NORTH SEA ECHOES, nothing new except for extending their first offering: heavier, more melancholic, more pervasive."A Time of Innocence and Purpose," with its bass and hypnotic, unsettling electro sample, is featured on LUNATIC SOUL. A beautiful ascent with Ray taking the lead, where things become much more interesting. A kind of GILDENLOW and pugnacious OSI hybrid, thanks to that captivating voice that makes all the difference. The ambient, intimate atmosphere makes you close your eyes and dream along to the edgy riff. "Enjoy The View" delves deeper into the electro-synthetic sound with its two-tone vocals and addictive instrumentation. The industrial riff, a sound effect on the thunderous breakdown, the keyboard undulating in a new dark-wave style. The magic works and endures with the energy of the invigorating chorus over the haunting verse, the haunting, dark outro. "Good Enough" features a crystalline, airy, stereo acoustic arpeggio reminiscent of the good old days. The raw, spoken-word vocals are laid over it, creating a country evening feel. The warm crescendo, with Ray as the sonic hero, evokes a dark Louisiana vibe with animals singing in the background: sublime and utterly simple, surfing on the atmospheric. "I'll Leave A Light On" kicks off with a fat riff, a melancholic nod to Katatonia. The pre-screamed vocals over the powerful sound, the chorus like something out of the mainstream era: the nostalgia is amplified by a punchy guitar solo bursting with notes. An added choir graces this track, which flows effortlessly, nothing new but well executed, finally on Fates Warning. "All Fall Away" boasts a bouncy bass beat. A dark, monolithic feel, redolent of Eurythmics in a heavy version, for this primal alternative drift. The guitar twists and turns, illuminating the space, the beat becomes oppressive, reminiscent of PARADISE LOST with Ray's voice, the chorus, then the beat abruptly stopping."Revenge," with its Wavy-esque guitar, surfs on the scales of THE CURE. This decadent rock descends to the realm of electro-pop, a softer DEPECHE MODE, Ray bribing his vocal cords. A repetitive, melancholic finale, far removed from prog rock. "Villains Or Saints" returns to mainstream, mainstream rock with its heavy melody, surfing once again on FATES WARNING. The haunting, synthetic rhythm builds and creates a heavy guitar space over the velvety keyboard. Ray conducts this masterful string piece, always effortless yet captivating, this timeless ballad. "What Is And What Was What," with its dark, ambient, mysterious intro and that wind that seems to come from nowhere. Vocals over a guitar arpeggio, choir over organ, hairs shiver. The bass resonates, clears the speakers, the pleasure of having this vibrant, body-piercing sound, like an arrow piercing your heart. "All That Comes After" returns to edgy rock, energized by its catchy melody. A B-side track that doesn't offer anything new, however, except perhaps to test the stereo image on the atmospheric drift. This melodic sound takes you back to the previous millennium. "How To Cast A Shadow" concludes, the new-wave vibe with its heady keyboard, as fat as the 'metroganic' drums, Ray weaving through this dark, hybrid, alternative slow jam. The mantra-like latency for dancing, swaying with his wife, the guitar both melancholic and slide-like. The feeling of navigating a bayou. A heavy guitar solo, the sound that makes you headbang, the refrain of 80s hard rock bands, I'm sucked into this musical spiral. The finale features Ray clinging to the primal synth, shh... Silence remains a constant presence throughout the album, with its enveloping notes.NORTH SEA ECHOES pushes their identity further with a heavy, dark approach, evolving with the addition of electronic elements to delve into the ghosts of the past, temptation, and reflection. (3.75)
items._genre: crossover prog / darkwave / industrial / electro-synthetic
items._cn_summary: NORTH SEA ECHOES 的第二张专辑延续并深化了首作的气质，整体偏重、更具忧郁感和渗透力。乐评反复提及电子合成器音色与暗潮氛围的运用，曲目在 electro-pop 与重型 riff 之间游走，借鉴了 Katatonia、Paradise Lost、Depeche Mode、The Cure 等乐队的影响。主唱 Ray 的声线被多次强调为专辑的核心吸引力，从低音呢喃到清亮领唱均能胜任。制作上注重空间感与层次，键盘波动、人声合唱和工业化音色片段交织，制造出沉浸式的听觉体验。不过乐评也坦承部分曲目'没什么新意'，属于对自身风格边界的巩固而非拓展。作为跨界前卫摇滚作品，它在暗潮和工业氛围上的渗透使其与用户的暗潮/电子偏好有一定契合度，但本质仍是旋律驱动的摇滚框架，未深入实验领域。

items.body: Old Europa Cafe releases four new albums and three reissues on 23 October 2026, all as limited digipak CDs. The Italian power electronics, noise and dark ambient label, founded in Pordenone in 1983 by Rodolfo Protti, groups the batch around three reissues from the catalogue of Atrax Morgue, two new records tied to Swedish musician Nordvargr, and new albums from Black Leather Jesus and The Rita’s back catalogue. Atrax Morgue’s ‘Alive and Dead’, ‘Paranoia’ and ‘Pathophysiology’ reissued Atrax Morgue was the project of Marco Corbelli, an Italian noise musician born in Sassuolo in 1970 who died in 2007. Working mostly with a Sequential Circuits Six-Trak synthesizer, Corbelli built his early catalogue on cassette through the industrial and noise “cassette culture” of the early 1990s, releasing on his own Slaughter Productions before moving to labels including Old Europa Cafe, Relapse and RRRecords through the late 1990s. Old Europa Cafe reissues three Atrax Morgue titles on 23 October. ‘Alive and Dead’ is a CD re-edition of a cassette the label sold out in 2018, remastered by Devi(L)s Granziera (Teatro Satanico) and adding two previously unreleased live recordings, from Treviso in 1999 and Tokyo in 2006. ‘Paranoia’, originally Atrax Morgue’s first full-length CD album, released on Old Europa Cafe in 2000, returns in an expanded edition remastered by Devis G., adding two alternate versions of the track “Il Forcipe di Thanatos” first issued on the 2017 “Malaplacenta” 7-inch; those alternate versions stem from a 2007 recording session, the year of Corbelli’s death. ‘Pathophysiology’, first released as a 1995 cassette and reprinted on CDr in 2002 and CD in 2019, is remastered again at Sweet Slaughter for this edition, with four previously unreleased bonus tracks, two recorded in 1995 and two in 2002. Nordvargr powers new Apex Parasite and Fistfun records Swedish musician Henrik Nordvargr Björkk, known as Nordvargr, recorded and contributed vocals to Swedish power electronics act Apex Parasite‘s new album ‘Warzone Europa’, tracked at Nar Mattaru over July and August 2026. The album is released as a hand-numbered edition of 199 copies. Björkk, also known for his work with Mz.412, Folkstorm and Bøltorn, also appears on ‘Not Nice Ever’, a harsh noise collaboration released as Fistfun with Claudio Frassine, known for his projects Mademoiselle Bistouri and North Central. ‘Not Nice Ever’ follows the pair’s earlier Fistfun release “Up the Rolls” and is limited to 199 hand-numbered copies. Black Leather Jesus and The Rita round out the batch American industrial power noise project Black Leather Jesus, founded by Richard Ramirez in 1989, releases ‘Probe’ in a limited edition of 300 copies. The album’s core lineup features Sean E. Ramirez, Nathan Golub, Thomas Puopolo, Richard Ramirez, Kevin Novak, JRL, Anjilla Ulfhednar, Scott Kindberg and Domokos, with individual tracks built around guest collaborations with slowdanger, G.X. Jupitter-Larsen, Yellow Gas Flames and The Rita. The Rita, the harsh noise project of Canadian musician Sam McKinlay, credited on Discogs with originating the “harsh noise wall” style and coining the term, also gets a reissue in the batch. ‘Possessed Nun Sleaze’ was first released in 1998 on Labyrinth Recordings, in an edition of 50 cassette copies, marking The Rita’s first release on an American label. Old Europa Cafe’s CD reprint carries new artwork and is dedicated to Isabella and Sister Angela.

items.body: Am I capable of writing about music without referencing Eurovision? I guess not, especially if the band in question legitimately competed in a recent edition of my beloved song contest. By charming over 76,000 voters with an atmospheric blend of Nordic folk rock, Gåte won the 62nd Melodi Grand Prix, subsequently leading to their appearance at the Eurovision Song Contest 2024, representing Norway. Despite moving on from their allotted semifinal, the group placed dead last amongst the twenty-five finalists. The chaotic performance of their song "Ulveham" didn't impress international audiences or the professional jury, but it sure as hell made an impact on one American Eurofan, and the consensus among hardcore watchers is that Gåte was brutally robbed. After their undeserved flop, Gåte retreated to the forests of Norway for two years, finally reemerging with Sigil—a grander full-length to rekindle the sylvan aura they condensed and presented to over a hundred million people in just three minutes. I like to think of Gåte like a wreath. The center is vocalist Gunnhild Sundli. Her vocalizations—whether singing or chanting—have an unmistakable inflection that drifts over each piece with both tenderness and command. When she dips down into her lower register, the atmosphere turns foggy, but when Sundli lifts her tones high she effortlessly clears the fog to reveal a lively forest. Her technique is perfect for this genre of folk rock, and probably the main reason for Gåte's longevity as a band. Adorning the surrounding area of the wreath are class-act musicians wielding an assortment of traditional instruments. Right-hand man Magnus Børmark plays guitar but also the Swedish nyckelharpa, drummer Jon Even Schärer handles all sorts of percussion, as well as a mouth harp, and Arent Todal tackles various stringed instruments. Further adding to the wreath (specifically to Sigil) is the legion of session artists. I may not be able to quickly discern Marit Aspås's cello from Olav Luksengård Mjelva's hardanger fiddle, but these instruments are key in creating the record's environment. Don't expect these instruments to shred at full capacity. Sigil is a slow burner, churning atmospheres with crescendos rather than jamming out. Although the ambiances Gåte builds are splendid, not a single song runs over five minutes long. This hinders what these ten songs could be. The best pieces like "Strandvaskar" pull off heavy-hitting, successful climaxes, while others like "Nokon" spend too much time creating the liftoff for a climax. I adore the slow songs, especially the pairing of ballads ending the album, and now that the band is on a bigger label, a more digestible approach to their wizardry is expected. But if Gåte's mission is to conjure grand images of Nordic myths and legends, packing it all into three-minute chunks probably isn't the right way to go about it. Sigil by Gåte

items._cn_summary: Gåte乐队以北欧民谣为底色，在专辑《Sigil》中调用大量传统乐器构建森林般的氛围。主唱Gunnhild Sundli的声线兼具低沉吟诵与高亢清亮，能够在不同音域间营造浓雾与清朗交替的听觉画面。乐队成员与客座乐手合作，将瑞典尼克尔哈帕琴、挪威哈当厄尔小提琴、口簧琴等多种斯堪的纳维亚传统乐器编织进摇滚框架，乐曲以渐进式渐强代替密集炫技。然而评论指出，所有曲目均控制在五分钟以内，限制了其史诗气质的延展，部分作品在铺垫上耗时过多。整体而言，这是一张扎根于地方传统、致力于召唤北欧神话意象的世界音乐作品。

items.body: 「世界3大ジャズ・フェス」に数えられるスイスのモントルー・ジャズ・フェスティバル（Montreux Jazz Festival）。これまで幅広いジャンルのミュージシャンが熱演を繰り広げてきたこのフェスの特徴は、50年を超える歴史を通じてライブ音源と映像が豊富にストックされている点にある。その中からCD、DVD、デジタル音源などでリリースされている「名盤」を紹介していく。 アブドゥーラ・イブラヒム、あるいはダラー・ブランド。アパルトヘイト下の南アフリカでジャズの演奏を始め、その後国外に逃れて音楽活動を続けた名ピアニストが91年の長い人生を終えたのは、今年(2026年)の6月だった。ソロ、デュオ、トリオ、コンボ、オーケストラと、あらゆるフォーマットで作品を残した彼の音楽のエッセンスに触れられるのが、1980年のモントルー・ジャズ・フェスティバルの記録『アット・モントルー』である。そのアルバムを紹介しながら、彼のキャリアを偲ぶ。 『アフリカン・ピアノ』の衝撃 ダラー・ブランドがイスラム教に改宗し、名をアブドゥーラ・イブラヒムとしたのは1968年である。彼の代表作として知られる『アフリカン・ピアノ』が、デンマークの首都コペンハーゲンでライブ録音されたのは69年だから、その時点で彼はすでにアブドゥーラ・イブラヒムになっていたことになる。しかし彼は、ダラー・ブランドとしてその後しばらく活動を続けた。 『アフリカン・ピアノ』の名義は、現行盤ではアブドゥーラ・イブラヒムとなっているが、長らくダラー・ブランド名義で流通してきた。ダラー・ブランドという名の方が現在でも通りがいいのは、ひとえに『アフリカン・ピアノ』の圧倒的な知名度による。 もっとも、ダラー・ブランドという名も実は本名ではなく、出生名をアドルフ・ヨハネス・ブランドといった。ダラーとは「ドル」のことで、南アフリカの故郷ケープタウンの港に寄港した水兵にドル札を渡してジャズのSP盤を熱心に収集していたことで、ダラーが彼のニックネームとなったのだった。 名作『アフリカン・ピアノ』の原盤権を当初持っていたのは、デンマークで1969年から72年までの短い期間活動したスペクテイター・レコードだった。73年になってECMのサブ・レーベルであるJAPOからリリースされたことで、このアルバムは広く世界に知られることになった。現在では、この作品はECMを代表するピアノ・ソロ作としての地位を不動のものにしている。アブドゥーラ・イブラヒムのほかのアルバムは聴いたことがなくても、『アフリカン・ピアノ』は何度も聴いたというジャズ・ファンはわが国でも少なくないと思う。 70年代初頭と言えば、モダン・ジャズが雑多な要素を吸収して鵺（ぬえ）のような音楽に変貌しつつあった頃だが、その時代でも『アフリカン・ピアノ』は奇異な作品であったと思う。延々と繰り返される反復フレーズ。スコールのように畳みかける旋律。隙間なく連続し、どこが始まりでどこが終わりか判然としない楽曲──。それは、アメリカのジャズ、あるいはアメリカの黒人音楽とは明らかに異質な音楽だった。 南アが生んだ3人の世界的ミュージシャン 現在聴くことができるアブドゥーラ・イブラヒムの最も古い録音は、ジャズ・エピッスルズというセクステットによるもので、レコーディングは1959年であった。このバンドには、やはりのちに世界的なミュージシャンとなるトランペッターのヒュー・マセケラも在籍していた。マセケラが「グレイジング・イン・ザ・グラス」で全米1位を獲得するのは68年のことである。 ジャズ・エピッスルズのメンバーのうち3人は、南ア初の黒人ミュージカル『キング・コング』に参加していて、マセケラもそのひとりだった。『キング・コング』のヒロインとして舞台に立ったのがミリアム・マケバで、彼女もまたのちに世界的シンガーとなる。マセケラとマケバは、わずか2年だが結婚していたこともあった。アブドゥーラ・イブラヒム、ヒュー・マセケラ、ミリアム・マケバ。南アが生んだこの3人のスターが同じコミュニティから出発したのは、南アのジャズ・シーンそのものが小さなコミュニティだったからである。 ジャズ・エピッスルズは、南アで公式に発売された初めての黒人ジャズ・バンドのレコードだった。『ヴァース1』がそのタイトルだったが、『ヴァース2』が録音されることはついになかった。アパルトヘイト下の南アにあって、黒人ならびにその音楽であるジャズに対する弾圧がほどなく激化したことがその理由である。 南ア独自のタウンシップ・ジャズ 1994年まで南アフリカの政権を握ったNP（国民党）が、悪名高い人種分離政策であるアパルトヘイトを掲げたのは1948年だった。南ア人は、「白人」「カラード」「インド人」「アフリカ人」の4つのカテゴリーに分けられ、結婚やセックスによる人種混淆を妨げる法律が整備されて、居住区の分割や都市における人種隔離が進められた。 人種の分類上、ヒュー・マセケラとミリアム・マケバは「アフリカ人」、アブドゥーラ・イブラヒムは白人と黒人の混血である「カラード」であった。3人はいずれも1960年代に母国をあとにしたが、その後マセケラとマケバが90年代まで一度も帰国が叶わなかったのに対し、イブラヒムは何度か国に帰ることを許されている。これは、「アフリカ人」と「カラード」の法的権利の違いによるものだったと思われる。 人種分離は、トイレ、レストラン、ホテル、劇場から、バス、学校、役場にまで及び、社会生活のあらゆる領域が「ヨーロッパ人」向けと「非ヨーロッパ人」向けに分けられた。「ヨーロッパ人」とは、南アへの初期入植者であるオランダ人と、その後入植してきたイギリス人を主に指す。 しかし、オランダ人とイギリス人の間にもまた格差はあって、南アの経済、政治、社会の上層を長らく支配してきたのはイギリス人だった。イギリス人支配に対するオランダ人のルサンチマンの結晶のような政党がNPで、その初期の構成員の多くは、戦時にあってナチス・ドイツを支持した者たちだった。政権を握った彼らが設計したアパルトヘイトの諸制度は、しばしばナチスのユダヤ人政策に比して語られる。 アパルトヘイトは、アメリカ南部で1860年代から100年間にわたって存続した人種差別法「ジム・クロウ法」にも似ていたが、それ以上に残酷であったのは、アメリカにはなかった黒人の強制移住があったことによる。 1923年に施行された原住民都市地域法という法律によって、黒人は「タウンシップ」と呼ばれた隔離居住区に住むことを強制された。最も古いタウンシップはイブラヒムの故郷であったケープタウンにあって、その後南ア全土にタウンシップが設けられた。ここで独自に発展したのが、タウンシップ・ジャズである。 アメリカのラグタイムやスウィングと南アの土着の音楽が混じり合って生まれたのがタウンシップ・ジャズで、そこにカリブ海の音楽の要素も感じられるのは、ニューオリンズを経由してもたらされた影響があったからかもしれない。また、南アはある時期までイギリスの旧植民地や入植地の共同体である英連邦の構成国であったから、同じく英連邦の国であったジャマイカやバルバドスから音楽が伝わるルートもおそらくあっただろう。 禁じられたジャズと音楽家たちの出国 1950年代になって、タウンシップ・ジャズと、その後に輸入されたアメリカのジャズをベースにしたジャズ・バンドがいくつか生まれた。ジャズ・エピッスルズがその代表格だったが、彼らが最初のアルバムをレコーディングしてほどなく、南ア史に残る事件が起きた。1960年3月21日の「シャープヴィル虐殺」である。 アパルトヘイト下の南アでは、黒人に身分証の常時携帯を義務づける「パス法」という法律があった。それに抗議するために南アの首都ヨハネスブルグ近郊シャープヴィルの警察署に集まった黒人群衆に警察が発砲した事件が「シャープヴィル虐殺」で、これによって69人が殺され、180人以上が負傷した。 反アパルトヘイト運動のリーダーであり、1962年に逮捕されて以後27年間を獄中で過ごしたのがネルソン・マンデラだった。アパルトヘイト撤廃後の新生南ア初の大統領に就任した彼の歩みを描いた映画『マンデラ 自由への長い道』に、シャープヴィル虐殺の場面が出てくる。犠牲者の多くは、警察の装甲車から逃げ惑う中、背後から無差別に撃たれたのだった。この事件は海外各国に衝撃を与え、国連は3月21日を国際人種差別撤廃デーと定めた。 この事件をきっかけに、南ア全土に抗議行動が広がり、それにともなって南ア政府の弾圧も激化した。ジャズの演奏やラジオでの放送も禁止され、ジャズ・エピッスルズは解散を余儀なくされた。その後、先の3人は故郷を後にすることになる。ヒュー・マセケラがロンドンに活動の場を移したのが1960年、アブドゥーラ・イブラヒムが欧州に移住したのが62年で、これはマンデラが逮捕されたのと同じ年であった。ミリアム・マケバは、反アパルトヘイト運動に関与した咎で、67年に国外追放されている。 サックス・プレーヤーとしてのイブラヒム 欧州に活動の場を求めたアブドゥーラ・イブラヒムの庇護者となったのが、デューク・エリントンだった。スイスにツアーで訪れていたエリントンにイブラヒムの演奏を聴くよう懇願したのは、彼の婚約者であったと伝わる。 イブラヒムのトリオの演奏を気に入ったエリントンは、この有望なピアニストのワールドワイドのデビュー作となる『デューク・エリントン・プレゼンツ・ザ・ダラー・ブランド・トリオ』のレコーディングを支援した。リリースされたのは、フランク・シナトラが1961年に設立したリプリーズ・レコードからだった。 その後イブラヒムは数々のアルバムをレコーディングすることになるが、最も多くのアルバムを残したのは、ドイツのレーベル、エンヤ（Enja）である。エンヤの設立は1971年で、これはECM設立の翌年に当たる。Enjaというレーベル名は「European New Jazz」の略で、この場合の「New」はアメリカのジャズに対して「新しい」のみならず、ECMよりもさらに「新しい」音楽を目指そうとする意気込みの表現でもあっただろう。 1980年、イブラヒムはモントルー・ジャズ・フェスティバルに出演して8曲を演奏した。うち6曲を収録したライブ盤がリリースされたのも、やはりエンヤからだった。 バンドは、アルト・サックス、トロンボーンをフロントに擁したクインテットだったが、冒頭の「ツァクヴェ」では明らかに3本の管の音が聞こえる。日本盤CDのライナーノーツには「3管を含むセクステットの一体感をアピールしている」という意味不明の記述があるが、3管に聞こえるのはイブラヒムもサックスを吹いているからである。 イブラヒムは、ピアノ以外にフルートやチェロなどを奏する多才な音楽家だった。モントルーではソプラノ・サックスを吹いていて、それがたんなる余技とは言えないのは、6曲中3曲でピアノを弾かずにソプラノを吹いているからだ。裏ジャケットのクレジットも「Soprano Saxophone, Piano」と、サックスが先になっている。 アルバムの最後の曲「イシュマエル」は、ベースの反復フレーズが延々と繰り返されるイブラヒムの代表曲のひとつだが、この曲で彼は堂々たるサックス・ソロを披露していて、吹き終えたのち、客席から大きな喝采を受けている。 イブラヒムの音楽の広大な世界 モントルーのライブ盤はわずか6曲だが、驚くほど多様であったイブラヒムの音楽がこの一枚に凝縮されていると感じる。タウンシップ・ジャズ、サンバ、アラビア音楽、デューク・エリントン、セロニアス・モンク──。これも彼の代表曲である「ザ・ウェディング」は、雑多な原料を混ぜ合わせ、それを蒸留したのちに残った原酒のように澄明で美しい。 アルト・サックスのほかにフルートも吹くカルロス・ワードはパナマ出身のプレーヤーで、ジョン・コルトレーン、ドン・チェリー、セシル・テイラーらとの共演で知られている。イブラヒムとは、ドン・チェリーとのトリオで録音した1972年のライブ盤『第三世界＝アンダーグラウンド／The Third World-Underground』からのつきあいであり、その後デュオ作も一緒にレコーディングしている。 『第三世界＝アンダーグラウンド』は何度も繰り返し聴きたくなる名作である。チェリーの個性が大いに発揮されているが、とくにアヴァンギャルドな作品ではない。このアルバムと、ソロ作の『アフリカン・ピアノ』、さらにオーケストラと共演した何枚かの作品のうちのひとつ、例えば『アフリカ組曲／African Suite』などをこのモントルーのライブ盤と合わせて聴けば、アブドゥーラ・イブラヒムの広大な世界の概要を知ることができると思う。エンヤにレコーディングされたアルバムから10曲をセレクトした『プレミアム・ベスト』というCDもまた、格好の手引きとなるだろう。 2011年のモアーズ・フェスティバルにて 独唱によって閉じられた長いキャリア 2024年、アブドゥーラ・イブラヒムはロンドンのバービカン・センターでコンサートを行い、その演奏をレコーディングした。フルート奏者と、ベース／チェロ奏者とのトリオによるライブで、そのアルバムに『3』というタイトルがつけられたのは、トリオ演奏であるからだけではなく、アルバムが3部構成になっているからである。 1部には、ライブ前の無観客のホールで、8トラックのアナログ・テープ・マシンで録音した6曲が収録されている。資料によれば、この機材はエルヴィス・プレスリーがデビュー曲「イッツ・オール・ライト」を録音した際に使ったものであり、メンフィスのサン・スタジオにあったその機材を現在所有しているのは、ブラーのデーモン・アルバーンだそうである。そのテープ・マシンを、デーモンのスタジオからバービカン・センターに運んで録音が行われたのだった。 2部、3部は客を入れたのちのライブ演奏で、2部ではイブラヒムのヒーローであったエリントンの「イン・ア・センチメンタル・ムード」と、ジョン・コルトレーンの「ジャイアント・ステップス」、3部ではセロニアス・モンクの「スキッピー」を演奏している。 2部と3部には「リプライズ」と題されたピアノ・ソロの演奏が収められているが、注意深く耳を傾ければ、その中にジャズ・エピッスルズの名曲「ブルース・フォー・ヒューイ」のメロディを聴くことができる。「ヒューイ」はヒュー・マセケラの愛称である。南アのジャズの歴史をともにつくった古い友に対する変わらぬ友情をイブラヒムは示そうとしたのかもしれない。マセケラの死去から6年が経っていた。 2回目のアンコールで、イブラヒムはアカペラで歌を歌っている。アフリカの民族語と英語をまじえて歌われるその歌には、「伝達──幾世紀の歴史をもつ海運貨物の音」というタイトルがつけられている。何世紀にもわたって海運で運ばれていった貨物。それが何を意味するか、言うまでもあるまい。 このアルバムが、結果的にアブドゥーラ・イブラヒムの遺作となった。アフリカの奴隷貿易の歴史を歌う独唱で、イブラヒムは長いキャリアを閉じた。彼の新作がもはや聴けなくなった今、残された膨大な作品の森にあらためて分け入りたく思う。 文／二階堂 尚 『At Montreux』 アブドゥーラ・イブラヒム／ダラー・ブランド ■1.Tsakve 2. Whoza Mtwana 3. The Homecoming Song 4. The Wedding 5. The Perfumed Forest Wet With Rain 6. Ismael ■アブドゥーラ・イブラヒム(ss,p)、カルロス・ワード(as,fl)、クレイグ・ハリス(tb)、アロンゾ・ガードナー(b)、アンドレ・ストロパート(ds) ■第14回モントルー・ジャズ・フェスティバル／1980年7月18日   投稿 【アブドゥーラ・イブラヒム】長い歩みを終えた南アフリカの名ピアニスト ─ライブ盤で聴くモントルー Vol.69 は ARBAN に最初に表示されました。

items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评是为纪念南非钢琴家阿卜杜拉·伊布拉欣逝世而作，回顾了他1980年在蒙特勒爵士音乐节的现场录音专辑《At Montreux》。文章从他的代表专辑《African Piano》切入，探讨了这部作品在ECM/JAPO厂牌下发行的历程及其音乐特征：绵延反复的乐句、密集层叠的旋律、模糊的起止结构，被视为与美国爵士及黑人音乐截然不同的独特存在。乐评追溯了伊布拉欣从1959年与Jazz Epistles六重奏合作的早期录音，到1968年改宗伊斯兰教并更名的转变，并将他与休·马塞克拉、米里亚姆·马凯巴并称为南非社区出身的三位世界级音乐人。文章还详细梳理了南非种族隔离政策的历史背景、班图斯坦法案对黑人音乐家的压迫，以及由此催生的城镇爵士这一本土音乐流派，呈现了南非独特的音乐文化与政治处境的深层关联。

items.body:
A key presence on the New York scene over the past 30 years, trumpeter, composer, arranger, and bandleader Steven Bernstein has immersed himself in such a wide array of music with his bands Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, Diaspora Soul, Universal Melody Brass Band, Spanish Fly, Blue Campfire, and the Butler-Bernstein Hot 9 that his output defies easy categorization. A former member of The Lounge Lizards and Levon Helm’s Midnight Ramble Band, Bernstein has also composed works for film, theater, and dance in addition to doing arrangements for a diverse list of artists, including Lou Reed, Lee “Scratch” Perry, Allen Toussaint, Marianne Faithfull, Linda Ronstadt, Rufus Wainwright, Darlene Love, Mario Pavone, Bill Frisell, and John Lurie. His lengthy list of sideman credits includes appearances on recent recordings by Laurie Anderson (Heart of a Dog), Roswell Rudd (Trombone for Lovers), Mostly Other People Do the Killing (Loafer’s Hollow), Antony and the Johnsons (Turning), and Nels Cline (Lovers). He also continues to perform with Ray Anderson’s Pocket Brass Band, Omaha Diner, and the Kamikaze Ground Crew.

Born in Berkeley, California, Bernstein moved to New York in 1978. By 1990 he had joined The Lounge Lizards, appearing on the group’s 1991 release Live in Berlin (Intuition). Shortly before that, in 1988 he formed the trio Spanish Fly with slide guitarist Dave Tronzo and tuba virtuoso Marcus Rojas. By 1995, producer Hal Willner, a fan of Spanish Fly, enlisted Bernstein as arranger for the soundtrack to Robert Altman’s film Kansas City, which led to collaborations on numerous other Willner projects, including tributes to Bill Withers, Doc Pomus, and Leonard Cohen, among many others.

In 1996, Bernstein formed Sexmob with saxophonist Briggan Krauss, bassist Tony Scherr, and drummer Kenny Wollesen. It remains his primary vehicle for exploring the slide trumpet, a rare instrument that he picked up in a Woodstock guitar shop back in 1977. Over two decades of recording, the group has put their singular stamp on an eclectic list of tunes by the likes of Leadbelly, John Barry, Hoagy Carmichael, Paul McCartney, Duke Ellington, Prince, Kurt Cobain, the Rolling Stones, James Brown, Count Basie, Professor Longhair, and Nino Rota. The group’s latest album, in its 20th anniversary year, is Cultural Capital, the first Sexmob recording to feature all original compositions.

From 1999 to 2008, Bernstein contributed four recordings to John Zorn’s Radical Jewish Culture series on his Tzadik label – 1999’s Diaspora Soul (featuring members of The Lounge Lizards and Sexmob), 2002’s Diaspora Blues (featuring Sam Rivers), 2004’s Diaspora Hollywood (inspired by classic film composers and West Coast cool jazz), and 2008’s Diaspora Suite (a homecoming recorded with Bay Area musicians). Each project combined traditional cantorial songs and elements of jazz, blues, and rock.

Bernstein’s Millennial Territory Orchestra debuted with 2006’s MTO, Vol. 1, which featured large ensemble interpretations of songs by Stevie Wonder, Prince, and the Grateful Dead, as well as Benny Moten and Charlie Johnson and His Paradise Band. They followed with 2008’s We Are MTO, which included renditions of tunes by Fats Waller, Don Redman, Count Basie, and the Beatles. Their 2011 recording, MTO Plays Sly, was a tribute to the music of Sly & The Family Stone and featured the late P-Funk keyboardist Bernie Worrell along with guest vocalists.

In 2012, Bernstein joined up with New Orleans piano master Henry Butler in the retro-flavored Butler, Bernstein and the Hot 9. Their critically acclaimed 2014 Impulse! debut, Viper’s Drag, featured spirited renditions of Fats Waller’s title track along with tunes by Jelly Roll Morton and originals by Butler. The restlessly creative Bernstein continues to juggle several working bands. During a recent residency at The Stone in NYC, he performed with Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, Spanish Fly, Blue Campfire, and Universal Melody Brass Band.

Bernstein’s latest album is ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance (Royal Potato Family). In the liner notes, Bernstein mentions being enchanted by Burning Spear’s Garvey’s Ghost (Island, 1976) back in 1981, only realizing years later that it was a dub version of Marcus Garvey, Burning Spear’s Island release from the previous year. Since then, Bernstein has wanted to record an acoustic jazz trio album and have the results remade as a dub album. The first half of the release, ResoNation Trio, features Bernstein on trumpets, Scott Colley on contrabass, and Nasheet Waits on drums. To challenge himself, Bernstein eschews his main axe (slide trumpet) for this session and instead plays regular valve trumpet, G trumpet, and flugelhorn. The second half is called Ultra Resonance and features the first session tapes remixed and rearranged in dub fashion by longtime producer Scotty Hard, who also adds various keyboards, samples, and percussion to the mix. The former date is as spartan as the latter is dense, yet the two recordings (different though they are in concept and execution), are inextricably linked. I interviewed Bernstein in the summer of 2026, shortly after the release of ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance.

* * *

Troy Collins: You’ve been touring with Laurie Anderson the past few years, as documented by the recently released Let X = X (Nonesuch), which features Sexmob as Anderson’s backing band. What has it been like interpreting and rearranging her tunes for Sexmob, especially since Sexmob (in)famously doesn’t typically use pre-arranged tunes and/or setlists? And perhaps more importantly, how did this particular collaboration come about and what is working with Anderson herself like?

Steven Bernstein: Playing with Laurie has been a life-changing experience. She is completely about creation, being in the moment, acting on every inspiration, trying every idea and having fun. Her work ethic is legendary. Her ability to transform an audience is mastery. So being around her and that energy is just a powerful and positive situation. Even though a “show” is basically set once Laurie has decided on it (we are touring a completely different concert, different songs, different stories, different visuals, and a different “theme”) we/she are constantly making changes. Every show day we are at the theatre by 2:00 pm (she gets there at 11:00 am to start working with the lighting director) and we run every piece, whether a new idea comes from Laurie, me, another member of the band, a random sound that makes Laurie say “What’s that? Let’s try that in ‘___’.” Every idea is entertained and often added to the show.

The story of how this all started is beautiful. I’ve been around Laurie and known her at a distance for a long time, but the first time we really worked closely was doing Hal Willner’s Leonard Cohen show in Brighton in 2004. I arranged two songs for her, “The Guest” and “If It Be Your Will.” At Hal’s memorial she wanted to do Lou Reed’s “Gassed and Stoked.” I brought an arrangement that sounded just like the record and we played it through. She turned to me and said, “that sounds great, but I had another idea, I have this new loop” and she starts activating the loop with her violin bowing. It was a very “Laurie-style” loop: rhythmic, sonic, and not in 4/4 time. Tony and Kenny just drop in and start playing. It was grooving and effortless from the first sound. Laurie ended up testing positive for Covid and was unable to play the memorial, but a week later she calls and says how much fun she had playing with us. She said, “I’ve never had that feeling playing music” and that Warners is re-releasing her records and she was thinking of revisiting her older material (which she had never done), and asked would Sexmob play with her? You know my answer.

TC: Since you mentioned him, I’d be remiss to not ask about your years working with Hal Willner. The man’s various artist projects were significant touchstones in my development as a listener. I know he was a big fan of Spanish Fly – is that how you first met? And how did you become his go-to arranger for so many of his projects?

SB: I heard Hal’s Nino Rota record the summer of 1981 while visiting back home in Berkeley. Peter Engelhart, the legendary metal percussion maker played it for me (his daughters are some of my oldest and best friends). It changed my DNA! After that it became a thing. Who is Hal Willner? Where is Hal Willner? I did Night Music with Karen Mantler in 1989. I also played with Carla Bley, Bootsy, and Allen Toussaint on that show. Hal came up to me and said that he was a fan of Spanish Fly, that he’d been coming to our gigs at the Knitting Factory (lurking in the back I’m sure). He gave me his number and said that he would love to help us in any way he could. That led to him producing the first Spanish Fly record (on Knitting Factory records). It is a great Hal Willner production. Hal and I had very similar musical loves and ideas about music, he believed in me and kept offering me amazing opportunities. That led to a 25-year relationship. He could ask me to arrange for Elton John, Bill Frisell, Nick Cave, Lou Reed, Courtney Love, Robert Altman, Marshall Allan, U2 – it was always magic and natural. When I met him, it was pre-internet, and I would keep a pad of paper next to me during our phone conversations. His references could be Ernie Kovacs, Rahsaan, Allan Ginsberg, Martin Denny, Dorothy Parker, Anne Waldman, The Three Stooges, Gregory Corso, Fellini ... I did my best to keep up and learned a lot.

TC: Talking about Willner reminds me that you’ve done arrangements for more people than I can list, and the stylistic variety of artists is staggering. I’m curious if there’s ever been any job you feel you couldn’t or wouldn’t do?

To clarify, the beautiful thing about music is that someone else can take a song that seems unsalvageable and make something new from it that the original author may not have ever suspected was possible. Having just listened to a recent interview with Bill Frisell, I was reminded of his rendition of Madonna’s “Live To Tell,” which transforms what I would consider to be a lightweight pop song into a rhapsodic epic.

You are obviously capable of the same magic, but I wonder, have there ever been offers that you’ve refused based on the material or direction that someone wanted to go with it? Have you ever encountered a song that you felt was simply unredeemable?

SB: Well, there’s a funny story from about 8 years ago, at the beginning of Trump’s 1st term. It was a slow time (as often is the case for freelance workers) and I got an email from someone about arranging/producing some songs. The guy is a Sexmob fan, knows my work with Hal, and he has written some protest songs, tells me he thinks he can get Bono to sing on them, etc. He is not a professional musician, but this is his passion. He also has a vision of a performance piece situation, where the song is played while the listener goes down the “golden elevator” and walks somewhere else. We agree to a fee and he sends me the demo. He is playing rudimentary chords on the piano, and sings one verse, one chorus – it’s about 25 seconds. I call him and ask if there is more, he says no that’s the song. I explain that songs usually have a second or third verse, maybe a bridge, but he says no this is the song. I explain to him that it’s about 25 seconds, and if he wants it to work the way he is envisioning, (going down the elevator and walking) it needs to be at least 3 minutes long. He says, “Well do that Sexmob thing.” I talk to my wife and tell her that I don’t know if I can do this and she says “I thought you said you can make music out of anything.” So, I did and it ended up very cool!

TC: Well then, the obvious follow-up question to that is – did Bono sing on it?

SB: NO. A total pipe dream!

TC: Since we’ve been talking about arranging, I assume nothing is off limits in your own bands regarding your original tunes. Are there any pieces specifically written for say Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, or Spanish Fly that don’t translate as well from one band to the other, or do you compose your pieces so that any of your bands can perform them?

SB: Each piece is written not only for the band, but specifically for the players in each band. So, there hasn’t been much crossover. There is a piece I wrote as a commission during the pandemic that I played with Sexmob and MTO, but it really worked better as an MTO piece. But the very last phrase (the kicker) of the MTO end of night theme came from a Spanish Fly composition!

TC: Let’s move on to your new album. Your latest release for Royal Potato Family, ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance present two very different facets of your artistry – the former title finds you playing on valve trumpet and flugelhorn (instead of the ubiquitous slide trumpet) accompanied by bassist Scott Colley and drummer Nasheet Waits, while the later features Scotty Hard remixing the trio. How did this project come about and when did you first meet and work with Scotty Hard? It seems to me your working relationship with Hard goes all the way back to the very first Sexmob album, 1998’s Din of Inequity.

SB: This project came about because of a grant from the Shifting Foundation. The idea of creating original music with the orchestration of valve trumpet, acoustic bass, and drum set has been a dream of mine for a very long time. This particular vibrational intersection is not widely used, so the unknown possibilities are vast. On a musical/improvisational/technical level it has a very specific set of challenges, and it has taken me this long to feel ready to undertake this long-held desire. Scott Colley and Nasheet were always the musicians I wanted to do this with; I have known them both a long time, and they are veteran masters of spontaneous composition. Another long-held dream has been to create a dub version of an improvisatory instrumental record. I heard Garvey’s Ghost in 1981, and it changed my DNA. Once I started making my own records, I was just waiting for the right opportunity ... and this was it. The trio record is purely conversational and in the moment; back porch music with unlimited harmonic and structural possibilities. The time spent on this record was the decades of playing and writing that preceded it. Ultra Resonance is a mirror image, in that Scott creates his pieces layer by layer, adding and subtracting sounds and rhythms – it takes weeks to build a track.

When I first started playing in The Lounge Lizards with Michael Blake on tenor, Scotty started coming to hang; he was a friend of Michael’s from Vancouver. The first session we did with him was for a Justin Warfield record on Quincy Jones’ label Qwest. It was produced by Prince Paul (I am a huge fan of De La Soul). Scotty wrote the horn chart and engineered. Scotty went on to record and produce the first four Sexmob records. I was already doing fast cuts and dropouts live, but Scotty’s mixes/arrangements shaped the sound of the band.

TC: Having just listened to Sexotica (Thirsty Ear, 2006), your collaborative effort with the production duo known as GoodandEvil (Danny Blume and Chris Castagno), I’m curious how that experience was compared to your similar efforts with Scotty Hard? How does GoodandEvil’s working method differ from Hard’s and what are your thoughts on the different outcomes?

SB: Regarding the two albums/processes – they were fundamentally different as working methods and outcomes. We went into Sexotica (which got a Grammy nomination) with the idea of creating a project that was half acoustic and half electronic. Sexmob went on and recorded all the compositions (two of them being loose jams with input from Danny Blume). Then we did a full day of overdubs with Kenny: wood percussion, metal percussion, bird whistles, and gongs. Then GoodandEvil did their magic. Some pieces skewed more acoustic, some more electronic. The idea was an even balance overall.

With Ultra Resonance Scott was given all the tracks (20 songs). The first track he made, “Titano,” was a piece that’s not on the trio record, but I felt it would be a good piece for Scotty to put his magic on. I figured he would do a “remix” of it, but he rewrote the bass line and created a brand-new piece (natch). After that it was just letting Scott experiment and follow his muse. We had mapped out a series of “zones” we wanted the pieces to be in, but everything Scotty created was totally unexpected. Part of this was the idea of intentional experimentation – on both of our parts. For me it was the idea of the acoustic record, for Scotty it was some new boxes/plug-ins that he had recently received, and the idea of not going back to his tried-and-true techniques. Also, with Sexotica I was not involved in their process, but with Scotty I would hang in the studio once the “track” was created, and was involved in arranging process (Scott claims I had 3 good ideas, I’d say more like 7.6).

As far as my thoughts on the outcomes – two singular recordings that I believe are unlike anything else in the modern recording world. I’m proud of that.

TC: Switching gears slightly (towards acoustic sounds), you’re a fan of vintage horns. I’m assuming that there are certain models you never take on tour and some that you take on the road more frequently? What are the criteria for those distinctions? And what about the slide trumpet? I’m not familiar with anyone else playing one, so where and when did you ever find one?

SB: Vintage trumpets aren’t an issue on the road. I just use the horn best suited for the music. The horn I used touring with Levon Helm was a handmade Chicago Benge from 1947. That was a horn that could project over a five-piece horn section and two electric guitars. It had amazing response and Levon could feel my beat matching his. That’s not what I need with Laurie Anderson!

Regarding the slide trumpet – I found my first horn in a guitar store in Woodstock in 1977 when I was attending Creative Music Studio. When I started Sexmob 30 years ago my old friend (and master repairman) Dick Akright in Oakland (who I met in 6th grade) built the horn I use. It’s one a kind! I’ve collected almost every brand of slide trumpet over the years, though they are not as playable as my horn.

The first horn was $25, at the time (mid-70s) and many trumpet players had one because they were cheap and easily available.

TC: Speaking of Levon Helm, what was it like working with Helm and how did that relationship come about?

SB: This is a long story. I knew Levon had been having “rent party” gigs at the barn. Tony Scherr had done some, and Erik Lawrence did as well. Levon was in danger of losing the barn, as this was a last-ditch attempt to raise some money and also make some music. Erik had invited me to play a few times, and there was a Saturday where I was available (I often did a wedding on Saturday, as I was raising a family, and those gigs paid the bills). Anyway, they mention a few songs Levon might want to do (no Band songs) and said come up early because we might rehearse. We got up there and Levon didn’t come out, so I sat with a boombox and learned a few more songs that Levon “might want to do.” It was a nice chill hang up there, and when it became clear that there was not going to be any rehearsing, I told Erik Lawrence “Don’t play what I play. You just play what you hear, and I’ll play what I hear.” That way we were both free to react to the music. We were playing with Olabelle, and Levon just walked up and got behind the drums. It was the most natural improvisation/spontaneous composition. Levon didn’t know my name, had never seen me before, just smiled at me and told me what he needed with his drum fills. It was magic, and in true Levon form, he put a song from that night on one of his CD’s. Pure improvisation – we had never met!

As far as working with him – it was some of the most magic, swinging, joyous, pure music I have ever had the opportunity to create. He taught me so much about playing in time, playing melody, playing directly from the heart to the people. He was as great and real and no bullshit and smart as you would think from his legendary status. And we had FUN. And he went from almost losing everything to winning three Grammys in eight years!

TC: Speaking of legendary performers, how did you meet pianist Henry Butler, and what was your working relationship with him like?

SB: Another long and beautiful story. In the summer of 1984, I was working with the Flying Karamazov Brothers. We spent two months doing a show at the Goodman Theater in Chicago, and then went on to do a second show at the Olympic Arts Festival in LA. When that was over, they invited me up to the Eugene Country Fair, a legendary hippie festival that was associated with Ken Kesey and the Grateful Dead family. When they asked if I’d like to join them on the Old Time New Age Chataqua tour, a traveling group of “New Vaudevillians” – musicians and environmental activists that toured small communities in the rural Northwest, camping out and putting on shows – that seemed like a better option than returning to my non-air-conditioned fifth story walk up apartment on 109th street in July.

Our first stop was our one actual “gig,” at the Vancouver Folk Festival, and we headed up there directly from the Eugene Country Fair, where we had been enjoying the kind of quality research one would associate with the Grateful Dead Community. As we entered the festival, I heard a sound I was not expecting at a folk festival – a piano player, playing and singing music that seemed like it was completely futuristic, and at the same time playing music that seemed to come from early pre-jazz America. I had never heard anything like this, and at first, I thought my ears and brain were still vibrating from my Country Fair adventures, but it was actually being played, and it was (a pre-Impulse records) Henry Butler. He completely changed my DNA and I became a fan, buying his records when they came out.

When the Kansas City soundtrack record came out on Verve records, it was a time of flowing money in the record business, CDs were selling, and I believe the Bertleman Family had bought the Verve company. In 1995 they organized a cross-country tour with the Joe Henderson Trio, Charlie Haden Quartet West, and the Kansas City All-Stars, which included many Verve artists. I was the musical director of a band that included David “Fathead” Newman, Don Byron, Nicholas Payton, Christian McBride, James Carter, Mark Whitfield, etc.

I had contracted the band but was unable to find a piano player (Gerri Allen and Cyrus Chesnut had done the movie). I contacted seemingly every pianist in NYC who would fit the bill, and none were available, and I was starting to panic. I called Hal Willner to ask his advice and without missing a beat he said “did you call Henry Butler?” And that’s how it all started.

Henry and I were kindred spirits and when the tour was over he told me we would work together again. In 2011 I was doing an “MTO Plays the Early Blues” concert at a summer series in NYC. The promoter, Jay Weisman, asked if I’d like to have Henry Butler play, and I said of course, but where is he? It turned out he had an apartment in Brooklyn, post Katrina. When the concert was over Henry called me and said we should do a show with MTO playing all of his music – that was the birth of Butler Bernstein and the Hot 9 (there were 10 people in the band). As far as my working relationship, he totally trusted my bandleading instincts and arranging, and I was always awed and inspired by the music flowing out of him.

TC: You bring up a salient point. Around the time of the Kansas City soundtrack, there seemed to be a very healthy major label interest in jazz that benefitted musicians of all stripes, even those somewhat on the fringe (James Carter, Don Byron, David Murray, etc.), which to me, evoked the pre-Young Lions era, when major labels signed post-loft jazz artists like Anthony Braxton, Arthur Blythe, and Henry Threadgill.

Much has changed since then. I’m curious what your thoughts are on that phenomenon? How have you adapted to the changing fortunes of the recording business? And what do you foresee for the future?

SB: Well, the beautiful thing is that I have been DIY since the beginning. I think the budget of the first Spanish Fly record (which was on Knitting Factory Records) was 3K, and Hal Willner produced it! I personally have never really had a record contract where I was signed and had a budget. I’ve had a few independent contracts, and records funded by public and private grants. That is the way everything is now, so it’s just the way I’ve always been able to create new things. And that’s what it’s about, creating new things.

TC: In reference to creating new things, I’m curious about your thoughts on live performance versus studio recording. Studio recordings of Sexmob often feature a fair amount of electronic manipulation and remixing, much like Ultra Resonance. What are your thoughts on the difference between purely acoustic performances versus such heavily processed and studio manipulated recordings? Do you vary your approach towards playing depending on the situation?

SB: My feeling is that once Electric Ladyland and The White Album came out, there was no turning back. Even my albums that aren’t “heavily electronically processed” (aka produced by Scotty Hard) feature mixes that are very specific, often times emphasizing certain frequencies, the same way a painter will use certain colors to draw the eye. I believe a record should be a mind-altering listening experience. ResoNation Trio is also a studio record, although one that creates a vision of an imagined acoustic experience. As far as playing, I just do the best I can when the recording light is on!

TC: Let’s go back to those early, heady days. According to your bio, you grew up in the Berkeley area and were friends with Peter Apfelbaum, with whom you regularly attended jazz gigs. There was mention of an “eye-opening gig” by the Art Ensemble of Chicago at San Francisco’s Great American Music Hall. What was it about that particular show that resonated with you?

SB: It was just seeing them live after listening to the records for two years. The magic and visceral-ness of it. There is magic that happens when you are in the room, seeing the musicians and feeling the vibrations, sharing the communion of music. We also met them that night. We were pretty heady. We went to their dressing room and banged out “Nfamoudou-Boudougou” on the door. They were certainly shocked to open the door and see two scruffy teenagers.

They welcomed Peter and me into the dressing room, and that started a relationship that continues to this day (Peter is still in touch with Roscoe). When I moved to NYC I went to see the AEC at the Public Theatre, either late 1979 or early 1980. Now when we went to shows in the Bay Area everyone was dressed hippie funky, so that’s how I showed up, probably in overalls and a t-shirt. I go backstage after the show and am totally self-conscious to be surrounded by well-dressed urban New Yorkers in Kente Cloth and immaculate jewelry. Lester opens up the dressing room door, peeks out at all the “beautiful people” and says “BERNSTEIN get in here!” closes the door, points to the table and says “you can roll a joint, right?” (I could).

TC: Now that’s funny. I certainly remember my one and only time seeing the Art Ensemble of Chicago. It was in Philadelphia, at The Clef Club. Jarman wasn’t touring with them at this point, but it was still magical, ceremonial even.

One group I regretfully never saw was The Lounge Lizards. You were a member of The Lounge Lizards in the 1990s. How did that association come about? And while bandleader John Lurie has had an unusual (to say the least) life and career path since then, I was wondering, do you still have any contact with him?

SB: I have yet another tall tale to tell. It was summer of 1989 and I was touring with Chautauqua again, the same group of people I was touring with when I first heard Henry Butler in 1984. Back then we had answering machines that you called into and used a beeper to retrieve your messages (This is pre cell phones). I was in a small town somewhere, probably Idaho or Montana, and I went to a payphone and checked my messages, and I heard a message from John’s assistant saying to call John up because he was interested in having me join The Lounge Lizards. Needless to say I was beyond excited, because The Lounge Lizards was the “Premiere Band” on the downtown scene.

I call John up and the first thing he says to me is “Do you have a suit?” The next thing he says to me is “you’re not gonna get a lot of solos.” Luckily, the tour was heading to a place of general civilization (Port Townsend) and I was able to put together a tape so John had an idea of what my playing was like, and that September I started rehearsing with the band.

I still talk with John. The most recent project we did together was working on music for his film, that was two summers ago. We did music for Painting with John, and there was an excellent and entertaining episode in season three (I believe) that featured the making of the soundtrack, which really showed the process that we use.

Early on with The Lounge Lizards I started to arrange and transcribe for John, first working on Fishing with John, which led to arranging and conducting soundtracks such as Get Shorty and Excess Baggage. Get Shorty was the summer of 1995, and John and I would spend 12 hours a day together as I transcribed his ideas and put them into notated forms.

TC: I’m glad to hear you’re still in contact with John. Speaking of the 1990s, you recorded four albums in the late 1990s to early 2000s for John Zorn’s Radical Jewish Culture series on his Tzadik label: Diaspora Soul (1999); Diaspora Blues (2002); Diaspora Hollywood (2004); and Diaspora Suite (2008). As a fan of those albums, I’m curious if you ever return to any of those tunes or arrangements?

SB: I’m glad you brought up those records. I love the Diaspora series too. Yes, it lives on. I wrote big band arrangements of some of this music for Arturo O’Farril and the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra for two different concerts. I arranged a version of “Ani Mamin,” which I recorded with saxophones and valve trumpet on Diaspora Soul, reimagined as a tribute to Eddie Palmer and Conjunto Libre, arranged now for four trombones and slide trumpet. I learned that Barry Rogers, the architect of the New York salsa trombone sound, was raised in Brooklyn and his father and uncle sang with Moshe Kousevvitskey’s choir. Full circle New York history for you. I also recorded a version of “Cha” with Arturo and the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra. We recorded it during the pandemic, so it's all over-dubbed. “Cha” was inspired by John Zorn’s composing for Masada, and I created an arrangement inspired by Machito. I recently revisited the Diaspora Blues music alongside Arturo O’Farrill, Anat Cohen, and a small version of the Afro Latin Jazz Ensemble. This October at the Stone I'll be premiering a duo version of the Diaspora music with Arturo O’Farrill, so the music lives on, and keeps evolving.

TC: What other musical projects or performances do you have coming up in the near future?

SB: Here are a few upcoming shows:

September 23-29: Laurie Anderson and Sexmob, West Coast Tour and Chicago October 1: Helm Family Ramble in Brooklyn October 2: ResoNation Trio at Tempo, Kingston NY October 28: ResoNation Trio at The Stone October 29: Ultra Resonance at The Stone October 30: Diaspora Special Edition with Arturo O’Farrill at The Stone October 31: Sexmob Kurt Weill Halloween at The Stone

Sexmob Live at Carambolage, Bolzano (the last night of our March 2026 European tour) will be released at the end of the year. It’s our first documentation of the “new sound” of the band with Kenny’s electro drums in the mix.

And more upcoming projects that I’m not quite ready to announce.

items.body: If music unlocks the heart, then A Baleia (which means ‘The Whale’ in Portuguese) is a subtle rotating of the key, a 22-minute selection of soulful tape-recorded soundscapes. Will Samson’s latest album crafts kind, instrumental music, its soft, lulling tones originating from a state of deep relaxation and tranquil, limitless motion. Last summer, Samson spent some time in a flotation tank – a soundproofed pod where one floats in salted warm water while at the same time experiencing total darkness and weightlessness. This experience proved to be deeply healing and therapeutic, and these sensations ripple through the music, submerging it in a tide of sensuous strings and slow-moving atmospheres. Paradoxically, the music glows warmly as it lies in the dense depths of darkness. A feeling of unrestricted freedom is able to turn the locks of an ashen heart until it wakes up, changing its key, transcending into overwhelming euphoria. This is a utopic experience, but it’s a mere illusion, an imitation played out in the rigid confines of a cube, and that’s okay. That’s more than okay. You’re free, unattached to the world and its pressures, severed from its umbilical cord, a step out of reach from its outstretched, lingering hand. The music feels both detached and intimate, at once wrapped up in and removed from its surroundings. When the eyes open, they stare into the darkness. When the lids close, everything lights up. The music is in the world, but the pause button has been pushed, its license to pressurize and demand fully revoked. Soaking in the soothing texture is something close to bliss. The world continues to exist, and it continues to speak, but things are tuned out of range, like quiet voices coming from another room or a radio with its volume turned down. Senses are heightened. Featuring violin from Beatrijs De Klerck and Matt Resovich (of The Album Leaf), Samson also collaborates with Brumes and Benoit Pioulard, forming something of an ambient dream-team. The strings swell and meander, brushing against the gently-breathing body of music like eels slow-dancing in the deep. Under the water, everything’s unclothed, and strict regularity disappears. The music loosens, becomes elastic as it kisses the depths, with only a drum occasionally keeping up an appearance of perfect time, supporting and upholding the music’s bone structure. Other than that, the gloopy, brightly coloured tones drip like honey as they splay out their tones / arms, floating in life-giving waters. Like a mermaid’s song, sugar-sweet feminine sighs and vocals emanate from within. Sometimes in the ascendency, as if rising up on the tip of a bubble, and sometimes drooping like a shipwreck, Samson’s music is the sound of ambient freedom. Things are better down where it’s wetter. Release date: 18.05.18. www.dauw.bandcamp.com
items._genre: ambient / drone / tape music / experimental folk
items._cn_summary: Will Samson的《A Baleia》是一张仅22分钟的氛围磁带录音作品，灵感源自他去年夏天在隔音浮力舱中体验黑暗与失重感的疗愈经历。专辑以小提琴、合成器铺陈出缓慢流动的音景，整体质感柔和、温暖而空灵，宛如深海中漂浮的低语。Beatrijs De Klerck、The Album Leaf成员Matt Resovich、Brumes与Benoit Pioulard等多位合作者参与创作，弦乐在缓慢的节拍骨架上蜿蜒游走，旋律碎片像蜂蜜般缓缓滴落。作品中偶尔浮现女声叹息式的哼唱，类似美人鱼的歌声飘荡在水下。整张专辑呈现出一种从外部世界脱离后的自由感——暂停键被按下，所有压力消失，听觉反而变得敏锐。作为一张融合了磁带质感、器乐氛围与梦幻人声的小众独立发行作品，它在用户偏好的实验与电子领域有一定契合度，但更偏向氛围冥想方向，实验性元素相对克制。

items.body: Sudan Dudan is a Norwegian duo, Marit Karlberg and Anders Erik R�ine, who have released four albums over the last twenty years. On M�rke refrenger , their fifth, they are joined by Hans Hulb�kmo and Magnus Skavhaug Nergaard, contributing instrumentally and with the production. There are eight songs on the album with accompaniment principally led by acoustic guitar, augmented by fiddles, langeleik, lyre, jaws harp and more. The opening track, �Gard og grind� (�Fence and gate�) is a fine introduction to what is to come: finger-picked acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and snare-drum played with brushes leading into the harmonized vocal, together creating an alluring sound drawing the listener in. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The mood of the album, reflected in its title which translates as �Dark Refrains,� is not always dark, but most of the material, including the title track, certainly has a reflective quality. According to the press release �the lyrics smoulder with unease about the present and the future, while looking back to the myths and riddles of the past. They speak of the earth, the sun, the moon, stars and planets, of lost brothers, quarrelling sisters, loss and grief, of the power of imagination, and of the answers to the simplest and most difficult riddles.� The lyrics of all the songs, in Norwegian, are included in the sleeve notes and while a hasty online translation can aid with some understanding, the full meanings tend to remain cryptic, but there is a sense that words and music complement each other. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan For all its dark moodiness, M�rke refrenger does have its lighter moments. �Bagatelle� recalls and reinvents the melody of a well-known French song, adding some off-kilter harmonies, while �Rulleball� is more characteristically Norwegian, employing a vocal style known as tralling in which words are replaced by a vocalization of the melody, originally used to accompany dances when no instrument was available. No translation necessary there. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The final track �Skriften p� veggen� (�the writing on the wall�) features, for the only time on the album, electric guitar. The sound is deep and twangy, shades of Duane Eddy or a David Lynch soundtrack and it works very well. All in all a fine, imaginatively conceived and beautifully produced record, available as a download or vinyl. Find the artists online. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由挪威二人组Sudan Dudan与Hans Hulbøkmo、Magnus Skavhaug Nergaard合作完成。八首曲目以原声吉他为主，辅以小提琴、langeleik琴、里拉琴、口簧琴等北欧传统乐器，部分段落加入电吉他。歌词以挪威语撰写，探讨对当下与未来的隐忧，回望神话与谜语，主题涉及大地、星辰与失去的亲人。专辑在整体阴郁内省的氛围中穿插轻盈段落："Bagatelle"挪用法国旋律加以变形和声，"Rulleball"使用无词的tralling唱法。终曲"Skriften på veggen"以深沉的电吉他音色收尾，带有Duane Eddy式twang与David Lynch式悬疑气质。制作细腻，词曲互补，世界音乐元素明确，但实验性有限，属融合北欧民谣传统的精致之作。

items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.
